title: Igris
description: Igris is a governed execution system for AI workloads. It runs across cloud, edge, and robotics hardware — every execution is bounded, verifiable, and resilient.
content: Igris One System, Three Surfaces Cloud Edge Robots What Igris Guarantees Where to Start Platform Guarantees # Igris Igris is a governed execution system for AI workloads. It runs across cloud, edge, and robotics hardware — every execution is bounded, verifiable, and resilient. --- ## One System, Three Surfaces ### Cloud Igris coordinates inference across multiple cloud providers. It selects the best provider for each request, handles failover automatically, and tracks cost. Your application uses a single OpenAI-compatible API and stays oblivious to which provider responded. ### Edge Igris runs on your hardware — a server, a Raspberry Pi, a Jetson — and serves local inference without internet access. The same API, the same governance model. Data stays on device. ### Robots Igris connects to ROS2 ecosystems and executes AI-driven missions on physical hardware. Fleet coordination, safety limits, and execution receipts apply to robotic agents the same way they apply to cloud workloads. --- ## What Igris Guarantees **Bounded execution.** Every request runs inside declared resource limits. Token budgets, time limits, tool restrictions, and capability gates are enforced at the engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. **Verifiable records.** Every execution produces a cryptographically signed receipt. Inputs, outputs, resource use, and capability grants are recorded and tamper-evident. **Resilient inference.** When cloud providers are unavailable, Igris falls back to local on-device models automatically. Your application sees the same response format either way. **Agent capabilities.** Igris runs reflection agents, planning agents, multi-agent swarms, and behavior trees. Tool use — HTTP, shell, filesystem — is governed and auditable. --- ## Where to Start | Goal | Start here | |---|---| | Make your first request | [Quick Start](/docs/quickstart) | | Understand the execution model | [Execution Model](/docs/execution-model) | | Run AI agents | [Agents](/docs/agents) | | Deploy on a robot or edge device | [Robotics](/docs/robotics) | | Coordinate a cloud fleet | [Cloud Coordination](/docs/cloud-coordination) | | Audit and compliance | [Audit](/docs/audit) | | SDK and language clients | [SDK](/docs/sdk) | --- ## Platform Guarantees **Bounded execution.** Resource limits, capability gates, and time budgets are enforced at the engine level. **Verifiable records.** Signed execution envelopes cannot be altered after the fact. Every decision is re

content: Agent Lifecycle States State Transitions Querying Agent State Get current state of all agents Get a specific agent Lifecycle Records Force Termination Safe Idle (Human-in-the-Loop) Recovery # Agent Lifecycle Every agent running on the execution engine has a tracked lifecycle. State transitions are deterministic, signed, and queryable — giving you a full audit trail of every agent's history from initialization to termination. --- ## States | State | Meaning | |---|---| | `INIT` | Agent registered, not yet started | | `RUNNING` | Actively processing a request | | `IDLE` | Waiting for the next request | | `DEGRADED` | Repeated failures; execution continues with reduced confidence | | `SAFE_IDLE` | Paused pending human review or approval | | `RECOVERING` | Restarting after a violation or crash | | `TERMINATED` | Permanently stopped; no further requests accepted | --- ## State Transitions INIT → RUNNING RUNNING → IDLE (request completed normally) RUNNING → DEGRADED (error threshold exceeded) RUNNING → SAFE_IDLE (human approval required) IDLE → RUNNING (new request received) DEGRADED → RECOVERING (recovery triggered) RECOVERING → IDLE (recovery succeeded) RECOVERING → TERMINATED (recovery failed) SAFE_IDLE → RUNNING (approval granted) SAFE_IDLE → TERMINATED (approval denied) * → TERMINATED (explicit shutdown or fatal error) --- ## Querying Agent State bash # Get current state of all agents curl http://localhost:8080/v1/agents \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # Get a specific agent curl http://localhost:8080/v1/agents/agent-abc \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "state": "IDLE", "created_at": "2026-03-01T10:00:00Z", "last_transition": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "total_requests": 47, "violations": 0 } --- ## Lifecycle Records Each state transition is recorded as a signed lifecycle event: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "from_state": "RUNNING", "to_state": "IDLE", "trigger": "request_completed", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "signature": "sha256:d4e1..." } Lifecycle records are hash-chained and included in the audit log alongside execution receipts. --- ## Force Termination bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/agents/agent-abc/terminate \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" A forced termination is recorded with the requesting identity and timestamp. --- ## Safe Idle (Human-in-the-Loop) When an agent enters `SAFE_IDLE`, it pauses execution and waits for an explicit approval signal. title: Agents
description: Igris supports four agent patterns: reflection, planning, tool use, and swarms. All run inside the execution envelope with full governance applied.
content: Agents Reflection Agents Planning Agents Tool-Use Agents Multi-Agent Swarms MCP Swarm Mode Agent Lifecycle Choosing the Right Agent Pattern Mode Flags Monitoring Agent State Context Engineering # Agents Igris supports four agent patterns: reflection, planning, tool use, and swarms. All run inside the execution envelope with full governance applied. --- ## Reflection Agents A reflection agent generates an initial response, evaluates its own quality, and regenerates if the quality score falls below a threshold. **Execution loop:** 1. Generate initial response 2. Score response on a 0.0–1.0 quality scale 3. If score ≥ threshold: return response 4. If score < threshold: regenerate with critique feedback 5. Repeat until threshold met or `max_steps` reached **Configuration:** json { "mode": "reflection", "reflection_threshold": 0.8, "max_reflection_steps": 3 } **When to use:** Tasks where response quality must meet a minimum bar before the result is returned — code generation, structured output, reasoning tasks. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Planning Agents A planning agent breaks down complex tasks into steps, executes each step, observes the result, and adjusts the plan before proceeding. **Execution loop:** Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect → Plan (repeat) The agent maintains a working plan that is revised after each step. Planning steps consume `max_steps` from the execution envelope. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "planning", "max_steps": 10 } **When to use:** Multi-step tasks where the approach depends on intermediate results — research, code generation with testing, multi-stage workflows. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Tool-Use Agents A tool-use agent can call external tools as part of inference: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. Tool calls are governed by the execution envelope's capability grants. Available tools (each requires an explicit capability grant): | Tool | Capability | What it does | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | GET/POST to external APIs | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands (sandboxed) | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, list files | Tool calls are recorded in the execution receipt including the call parameters, response, and latency. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "tools", "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": true } } [Tools →](/docs/tools) · [Capability Model →](/docs/capability-model) --- ## Multi-Agent Swarms A swarm executes a task using multiple specialized agents in parallel. Method GET Path /v1/account/api-key Base URL https://overture.igrisinertial.com Auth Session cookie or igris_ API key Surface Cloud API Stability stable Support core Deployment cloud ## When To Use Use this endpoint when you are auditing tenant access state, confirming whether an environment already has a key, or checking whether key rotation happened when expected. ## Integration Guidance Safe to retry on transient 5xx or 429 responses. title: API Authentication
description: Authentication models for cloud and local API use.
content: Authentication Tenant API Keys Session Cookies Runtime-local Auth Choosing a Credential Bearer Example Example JSON # Authentication Which credentials belong to automation, browser sessions, and runtime-local deployments, and how to choose the right one for each route. ## Tenant API Keys Customer automation should use tenant API keys with the `igris_` prefix. These keys are the default credential for server-side integrations, CI jobs, backend workers, and any script that is calling the hosted API outside the browser. Supply the key as `Authorization: Bearer ...` or `X-API-Key` if the endpoint allows it. Endpoint pages call out the expected model explicitly, so treat the endpoint page as authoritative over any generic assumption. ## Session Cookies Browser-driven console workflows use session cookies. These routes are designed for an authenticated user session rather than headless automation, so they should not be treated as generic bearer-token endpoints unless the endpoint page says an API key is also accepted. If you are building automation, prefer routes that are documented with API-key access. ## Runtime-local Auth The local runtime API follows the runtime `auth` configuration. Some deployments intentionally keep that surface inside a trusted network boundary with minimal local auth, while others front it with stricter controls. Because that access model depends on deployment, do not assume that a local runtime route behaves like the hosted API. ## Choosing a Credential Use tenant API keys for server-to-server automation. Use session cookies for browser experiences that are already inside the Igris console. Use runtime-local authentication only when the endpoint is explicitly local and you control the deployment boundary. ## Bearer Example text curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" \ https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/models ## Example JSON json { "error": "unauthorized", "code": "INVALID_API_KEY" } API authentication bearer api key session cookie runtime auth

title: API Errors
description: Error handling and common response codes.
content: Errors Status Codes Validation Errors Authentication Failures Server Errors Handling Strategy Error Envelope Example JSON Common Status Codes # Errors How to read error responses across the API reference and what to expect from validation, authentication, throttling, and server failures. ## Status Codes The HTTP status code tells you what class of failure happened before you look at the JSON body. Treat 4xx responses as request, authentication, or access problems that your client should handle directly, and treat 5xx responses as server-side failures that may require retry, fallback, or operator attention. The most common patterns are 400 for invalid request shape, 401 for missing or invalid credentials, 403 for an authenticated request that still is not allowed, 404 when the addressed resource does not exist, 429 when throttling is applied, and 500-level codes when the server cannot complete a valid request. ## Validation Errors Validation failures usually mean the request shape was wrong for the route you called. Many handlers return a compact JSON envelope with `error` and sometimes a more specific `message` or `code` value that tells you what part of the request could not be accepted. ## Authentication Failures Authentication failures typically return HTTP 401. Session-based handlers often use codes such as `MISSING_SESSION` or `INVALID_SESSION`, while API-key handlers more commonly return `INVALID_API_KEY`. ## Server Errors Server-side failures commonly return a generic error such as `internal_error` or a route-specific code such as `registration_failed` or `STORAGE_FAILED`. These responses indicate that the server accepted the route contract but could not complete the operation. ## Handling Strategy Good clients do not handle every error the same way. Fix the request for 400-class validation issues, refresh or replace credentials for 401 responses, stop and inspect authorization assumptions on 403 responses, and apply controlled retry or fallback only for the routes and statuses that are documented as retry-safe. ## Error Envelope text { "error": "invalid_request", "message": "Failed to parse request body" } ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 400 | Bad Request | The route was reached, but the request body, query, or path data did not match the endpoint contract. | | 401 | Unauth API errors error codes invalid request unauthorized internal error

title: API Introduction
description: Overview of the customer API contract.
content: Introduction Two Product Surfaces How Endpoint Pages Work SDK Guidance Support Labels and Deployment Modes Base URLs Example JSON # Introduction How the Igris API reference is organized, when to use each access point, and how to move from guides into endpoint-level integration work. ## Two Product Surfaces Igris is documented here as one product with two access points. Use the hosted API at `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` when your integration needs account, fleet, billing, receipt, or policy capabilities. Use the local runtime API at `http://localhost:8080` by default when the request belongs on the machine where Igris is running. This split is about where the request executes, not about two different products. The API reference groups endpoints by capability so you can navigate by task first and only think about the base URL when you are ready to make the call. ## How Endpoint Pages Work Every endpoint has its own page. That page tells you what the route is for, which authentication model it expects, the path and query parameters it accepts, the request body fields that matter, and the status codes you should plan for in a real client. Use the overview page to browse by capability, then switch to endpoint pages when you are implementing or debugging a specific call. ## SDK Guidance JavaScript, Go, and Rust are the first-class SDK languages today. When an endpoint is covered by a native SDK, prefer that SDK for application code because it gives you a cleaner call surface and reduces request-shape drift over time. Some management routes are still best treated as direct HTTP integrations. In those cases, the endpoint page is the primary contract: use the request and response examples, confirm the authentication model, and wire your own client behavior around the listed status codes. ## Support Labels and Deployment Modes Each endpoint page carries both a support label and a deployment mode. **Core** routes are the primary customer contract. **Supported** routes are part of the shipped product surface but may not be the first endpoint a new customer should start with. **Preview** routes are available, but they should be adopted deliberately. Deployment mode tells you where the route belongs operationally. **Cloud** routes are served by the hosted API, **Local** routes are served by `igris-runtime`, and **Hybrid** routes are used when the hosted product and one or more runtimes are working together. ## Base URLs text Cloud API https://overture.igrisinertial.com Local runtime http://l API introduction base URL surfaces overview contract

title: API Rate Limits
description: Rate limit behavior and retry expectations.
content: Rate Limits Global Control-plane Limit Runtime Download Limit Client Behavior 429 Example Example JSON Common Status Codes # Rate Limits What throttling exists today, where it applies, and how clients should behave when they receive a 429 response. ## Global Control-plane Limit The hosted API currently applies a default limiter of 100 requests per minute. Endpoint pages call out the exceptions that matter more than the global default. Response headers are only guaranteed on the 429 path right now. Clients should not assume that every successful response carries full rate-limit metadata. ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime download endpoints use a tighter subscription-aware throttle. Treat binary download as a provisioning or rollout action, not as a hot-path request that your application makes repeatedly during normal traffic. ## Client Behavior Build clients so that a 429 is expected and handled, not treated as an exceptional edge case. Honor `Retry-After` when it is present, apply backoff with jitter for repeated retries, and avoid running parallel request bursts that all wake up at the same second. ## 429 Example text Retry-After: 60 X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 429 | Too Many Requests | Retry after the advertised cooldown window. | API rate limits retry-after 429 throttle

content: POST /v1/vault/keys When To Use Integration Guidance Common Mistakes Related Endpoints Related Guides Request Body Request Example Code Examples cURL JavaScript Go Rust Sample Response Status Codes 400 Example 401 Example 500 Example # POST /v1/vault/keys Stores a tenant-scoped provider credential for hosted routing. The raw upstream key is encrypted on write, and later reads only return masked metadata so the secret does not become part of the ordinary control-plane surface. Method POST Path /v1/vault/keys Base URL https://overture.igrisinertial.com Auth Session cookie or igris_ API key Surface Cloud API Stability stable Support core Deployment cloud ## When To Use Use this endpoint when you are setting up or rotating hosted routing credentials for a tenant. It is usually one of the first administrative calls you make before sending production inference traffic. ## Integration Guidance Do not replay this request casually. Retry only on clearly transient 5xx or 429 responses, and make sure your client can tolerate the possibility that the first write may already have succeeded. ### Common Mistakes - Sending a raw provider name that is not part of the currently supported public identifiers. - Assuming a successful write means the key will ever be returned again in plaintext. - Using ad hoc key labels that make later rotation and operational ownership harder to understand. ### Related Endpoints - [GET /v1/vault/keys](/docs/api-reference/vault-policy-and-governance/get-v1-vault-keys) - [GET /v1/vault/keys/:provider](/docs/api-reference/vault-policy-and-governance/get-v1-vault-keys-provider) - [DELETE /v1/vault/keys/:provider](/docs/api-reference/vault-policy-and-governance/delete-v1-vault-keys-provider) ### Related Guides - [API Authentication](/docs/api-reference/authentication) - [API Errors](/docs/api-reference/errors) - [Key Management](/docs/key-management) ## Request Body | Field | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `provider` | `string` | Yes | Public provider identifier such as `openai` or `anthropic`. | | `key_name` | `string` | Yes | Human-readable label for the key record. | | `api_key` | `string` | Yes | Raw provider credential to encrypt and store. | ## Request Example json { "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "sk-live-redacted" } ## Code Examples ### cURL bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "sk-live-redacted" }' ### JavaScript javascript const response = await POST /v1/vault/keys Stores a provider key using `{ provider, key_name, api_key }`.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Approvals
description: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval pauses an execution run before it completes a high-stakes action. A reviewer must explicitly approve or reject the run before execution continues.
content: Human-in-the-Loop Approvals How Executions Get Paused for Review Finding Runs Waiting for Approval Reviewing in the Console Approving a Run → {"status": "RUNNING", "approved": true} Rejecting a Run → {"status": "REJECTED", "reason": "action_out_of_scope"} What Gets Recorded in the Receipt Replaying a Rejected Run → {"status": "replayed", "new_execution_id": "exec-01HABC"} Monitoring the Approval Queue Best Practices # Human-in-the-Loop Approvals Human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval pauses an execution run before it completes a high-stakes action. A reviewer must explicitly approve or reject the run before execution continues. The full approval event — who made the decision, when, and why — is recorded in the signed execution receipt and cannot be altered after the fact. --- ## How Executions Get Paused for Review The execution engine evaluates review triggers as each run progresses. Triggers are configured in your policy and can match on tool call targets, output classifications, capability combinations, or custom conditions. When a trigger fires, the run transitions from RUNNING to **PAUSED** with `pause_reason: human_review_required`. The run holds open in that state indefinitely — it does not time out and does not progress — until a human makes a deliberate approve or reject decision. The execution envelope remains intact while the run is paused. Resources are reserved and the agent's context is preserved. Once a decision is made, the run either continues (approve) or terminates (reject) from exactly the point where it was paused. --- ## Finding Runs Waiting for Approval Query paused runs via the API: bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/execution/runs?status=PAUSED" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "execution_id": "exec-01HXYZ", "agent_id": "agent-abc", "status": "PAUSED", "pause_reason": "human_review_required", "paused_at": "2026-03-31T10:14:22Z", "prompt_preview": "About to POST to https://payments.example.com/disburse with amount: 4500", "runtime_id": "runtime-01" } ] The `prompt_preview` field is a brief description of what the execution was about to do at the point it was paused. It is generated by the execution engine and is not the raw model input — it is a structured summary of the pending action, designed to give a reviewer enough context to make an informed decision. --- ## Reviewing in the Console The **Execution Runs** page in the console shows all paused runs in a dedicated review queue at the top of the list. Each row shows a **Review** badge and the time the run has been waiting. Click a paused run to open its detail panel. You will see: - **Prompt preview** — the pending action description - **Agent ID** — which agent initiated this run - **Pause reason** — always `human_review_required` for HITL items - **Paused

title: Deploying Igris on Edge Devices
description: Step-by-step guide for deploying the Igris runtime on Raspberry Pi, Jetson, and other edge hardware.
content: Deploying Igris on Edge Devices Supported Edge Platforms Install The Runtime 1. Download the archive 2. Extract and install 3. Download a model 4. Configure the runtime 5. Start the runtime Run As A Service Health And Monitoring # Deploying Igris on Edge Devices Running `igris-runtime` on edge hardware gives you local inference, local policy enforcement, and a clean path to hybrid cloud coordination. --- ## Supported Edge Platforms | Platform | Architecture | Minimum RAM | Recommended starting model | |---|---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4/5 | ARM64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano | ARM64 | 8 GB | Mistral 7B (Q4) | | Generic x86_64 host | x86_64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | GPU-backed x86_64 host | x86_64 | 16 GB | 7B to 8B GGUF | --- ## Install The Runtime ### 1. Download the archive bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-arm64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the checksum output before extracting. ### 2. Extract and install bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ### 3. Download a model bash mkdir -p /opt/igris/models wget -O /opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf \ "https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-gguf/resolve/main/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf" ### 4. Configure the runtime Create `/etc/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf", n_gpu_layers: 0, threads: 4, context_size: 4096 } } Platform tuning: - **Raspberry Pi**: keep `n_gpu_layers` at `0`; tune `threads` to the available CPU cores - **Jetson**: raise `n_gpu_layers` for GPU offload and keep `threads` conservative - **GPU-backed x86_64**: increase `n_gpu_layers` based on VRAM capacity ### 5. Start the runtime bash igris-runtime serve If you want the device to appear in Fleet, also set `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` before startup. --- ## Run As A Service Example `systemd` unit: ini [Unit] Description=Igris Runtime After=network.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=/home/igris/.local/bin/igris-runtime serve Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 User=igris Group=igris [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target --- ## Health And Monitoring bash curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health curl http://localhost:8080/

title: Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates
description: A practical guide to configuring capability grants, monitoring violations, and iterating on your agent policies.
content: Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates The Capability Model Available Capabilities Start Restrictive, Expand as Needed Step 1: Deploy with No Capabilities Step 2: Review Violations Step 3: Grant Legitimate Capabilities Step 4: Iterate Capability Patterns by Agent Type Read-Only Analyst API Integration Agent Automation Agent DevOps Agent Monitoring and Alerting Console Monitoring API Monitoring Setting Up Alerts Common Pitfalls Over-Granting Capabilities Ignoring Violations Not Using Shadow Mode # Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates When agents can make HTTP requests, execute shell commands, or access the filesystem, the risk surface grows significantly. Igris's capability gates ensure that agents can only perform operations you explicitly authorize. --- ## The Capability Model Every execution in Igris runs with a **capability grant** — a declarative list of what the agent is permitted to do. The engine enforces these grants before any operation executes. ### Available Capabilities | Capability | Controls | |---|---| | `allow_http` | Outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | Specific domains the agent can call | | `allow_shell` | Shell command execution | | `allowed_shell_commands` | Specific commands the agent can run | | `allow_filesystem` | File read/write operations | | `allowed_filesystem_paths` | Specific paths the agent can access | | `max_file_write_bytes` | Maximum bytes the agent can write | --- ## Start Restrictive, Expand as Needed The safest approach is to start with no capabilities granted and add them incrementally: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 1: Deploy with No Capabilities Deploy your agent with all capabilities disabled. Run it against real traffic in **shadow mode** to observe what it would do without actually executing. ### Step 2: Review Violations Check the **Proof → Violations** page in the console. Each violation shows: - Which capability was attempted - Which agent attempted it - When it happened ### Step 3: Grant Legitimate Capabilities For violations that represent legitimate agent behavior, grant the specific capability: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allowed_http_domains": ["api.example.com", "cdn.example.com"], "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 4: Iterate Repeat steps 2–3 until your agent operates without violations. This process typically takes 1–3 iterations for well-designed agents. --- ## Capability Patterns by Agent Type ### Read-Only Analyst An agent that analyzes data and produces reports: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } No tools needed. The agent works purely with its training knowledge and the provided context. ### API Integration Agent An agent that calls external APIs: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": tr

title: How Adaptive Routing Works
description: How Igris automatically routes requests to the best provider for your workload based on real-time performance data.
content: How Adaptive Routing Works The Problem How It Works Why This Matters for Your Workload Automatic Adaptation Handles New Providers Gracefully Balances Cost and Performance Configuration Monitoring # How Adaptive Routing Works When you configure multiple AI providers with Igris, you face a fundamental question: which provider should handle each request? The answer depends on constantly changing factors — provider latency, error rates, cost, and your specific workload patterns. Igris solves this automatically using an adaptive routing algorithm that learns from every request. --- ## The Problem Imagine you have three providers configured: | Provider | Avg Latency | Cost per 1K tokens | |---|---|---| | Anthropic Claude | 280ms | $0.015 | | OpenAI GPT-4 | 350ms | $0.030 | | Google Gemini | 200ms | $0.010 | A naive approach might always pick the fastest (Gemini) or the cheapest (Gemini). But what if: - Gemini occasionally times out under load? - Claude produces higher-quality responses for your specific prompts? - OpenAI is faster for certain model types? Static rules can't adapt to these dynamics. Igris's adaptive routing can. --- ## How It Works Igris maintains real-time performance statistics for each configured provider: latency, success rate, and cost. On each request, the routing engine selects the best provider based on recent observations — automatically balancing between providers it knows are reliable and occasionally trying others to keep its data fresh. After each request completes, the provider's statistics are updated with the observed result. A provider that performs well receives more traffic. A provider that degrades is automatically routed around. --- ## Why This Matters for Your Workload ### Automatic Adaptation If a provider's latency degrades, the router automatically reduces its traffic share. No manual intervention needed. When the provider recovers, traffic gradually returns. ### Handles New Providers Gracefully When you add a new provider, the router explores it to gather performance data, then settles into a steady pattern once it understands the provider's characteristics. ### Balances Cost and Performance The algorithm naturally finds the sweet spot between cost and performance for your specific workload. If a cheaper provider is "good enough," it will receive more traffic. If quality matters most, higher-performing providers dominate. --- ## Configuration Adaptive routing is the default. You can also select a specific strategy: json { "routing": { "strategy": "thompson-sampling", "fallback_chain": ["anthropic", "openai", "local

This page covers how to access, query, and export audit data. --- ## Execution Receipts Every execution produces a signed execution receipt. The receipt is the primary audit artifact. A receipt contains: - **Request identity**: request ID, tenant ID, timestamp - **Inputs**: full prompt, system message, and parameters - **Outputs**: full model response - **Resource usage**: tokens consumed, wall time, tool calls - **Capability grants**: what the execution was permitted to do - **Capability violations**: any operations that were blocked - **Tool calls**: parameters, responses, and latency for each tool invocation - **Signature**: cryptographic seal over the canonical envelope The signature is computed over a deterministic serialization of all fields. An altered receipt will have an invalid signature. [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) --- ## Lineage Each receipt includes a `request_id` that traces back to the originating API call. For executions that went through the cloud coordination layer, the `request_id` links the routing decision to the execution record: API call → routing decision (request_id: abc123) │ ▼ Execution receipt (request_id: abc123, provider: anthropic) │ ▼ Signed envelope (canonical hash: sha256:...) Full lineage is queryable end-to-end by request ID. --- ## Querying Receipts Receipts are queryable through two surfaces: - **Cloud API** (`overture.igrisinertial.com`) — the central execution ledger, accessible via the Proof API below - **Local engine API** (`http://localhost:8080`) — device-local storage; nothing leaves your infrastructure unless explicitly exported bash # List receipts via local engine curl http://localhost:8080/v1/receipts \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # Get a specific receipt by execution ID curl http://localhost:8080/v1/receipts/exec-01HXYZ \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # Filter by time range curl "http://localhost:8080/v1/receipts?from=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z&to=2026-03-02T00:00:00Z" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" --- ## Export Export receipts in bulk for external audit workflows: bash # Export as JSONL curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=jsonl&from=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -o receipts-2026-03-01.jsonl # Export as CSV curl "https://o

content: Behavior Trees 1. Cloud Definition Schema 2. Runtime Execution Schema Using the JavaScript SDK Using the Go SDK Practical Rule Durable Execution # Behavior Trees Igris currently exposes **two** behavior-tree schemas. Treat them as different layers of the product: - The **definition schema** used by the cloud control plane and console editor - The **runtime execution schema** used by the runtime API and native SDKs If you mix them up, validation will fail. --- ## 1. Cloud Definition Schema The coordination layer stores graph-style definitions using `nodes` and `edges`. json { "name": "shutdown-guard", "description": "Temperature-triggered shutdown sequence", "nodes": [ , , ], "edges": [ , ] } This is the schema used by: - `GET /v1/bt/templates` - `GET /v1/bt/definitions` - `GET /v1/bt/definitions/:id` - `POST /v1/bt/definitions` - `DELETE /v1/bt/definitions/:id` --- ## 2. Runtime Execution Schema The runtime and native SDKs use a nested tree representation with lowercase node types. json { "type": "sequence", "name": "shutdown-guard", "children": [ { "type": "condition", "name": "check_temp", "key": "sensor.temperature", "expected": "80" }, { "type": "action", "name": "shutdown", "tool": "http_post", "args": { "url": "http://localhost:9000/shutdown" } } ] } This is the schema accepted by the local runtime endpoints: - `POST /v1/btree/validate` - `POST /v1/btree/run` - `POST /v1/btree/deploy` --- ## Using the JavaScript SDK typescript import { Runtime, BehaviorTree, SequenceNode, ConditionNode, ActionNode, } from '@igris-inertial/sdk'; const runtime = new Runtime( ); const tree = BehaviorTree.fromJson( new SequenceNode('shutdown-guard', [ new ConditionNode('check_temp', 'sensor.temperature', '80'), new ActionNode('shutdown', 'http_post', ), ]).toJSON(), runtime, ); const result = await tree.validate(); console.log(result.valid); --- ## Using the Go SDK go package main import ( "context" "log" igris "github.com/igris-inertial/go-sdk" ) func main() { runtime := igris.NewRuntime("http://localhost:8080") treeDef := igris.NewSequenceNode("shutdown-guard", igris.NewConditionNode("check_temp", "sensor.temperature", "80"), igris.NewActionNode("shutdown", "http_post", map[string]interface{}{ "url": "http://localhost:9000/shutdown", }), ) tree := igris.NewBehaviorTree(treeDef, runtime) if _, err := tree.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } --- ## Practical Rule Use `nodes` / `edges` only when you are talking to the cloud definition API. title: Capabilities & Limits
description: The execution engine enforces a capability model: every execution runs with an explicit set of permissions. If an agent tries to do something outside those permissions, the operati
content: Capabilities & Limits Capability Fields Configuration Enforcement Points Violation Records Violation Types # Capabilities & Limits The execution engine enforces a capability model: every execution runs with an explicit set of permissions. If an agent tries to do something outside those permissions, the operation is blocked before it executes and the violation is recorded in the signed receipt. --- ## Capability Fields | Capability | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `allow_http` | bool | Allow outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | string[] | Allowlist of domains for HTTP calls | | `allow_shell` | bool | Allow shell command execution | | `allow_filesystem` | bool | Allow filesystem read/write | | `max_file_write_bytes` | int | Maximum bytes the execution may write | --- ## Configuration Set capability limits in your `config.json5`: json5 { capabilities: { allow_http: true, allowed_http_domains: ["api.openweathermap.org", "api.github.com"], allow_shell: false, allow_filesystem: true, max_file_write_bytes: 1048576 // 1 MB } } Capabilities can also be set per-request via the `X-Igris-Capabilities` header for tenants with override permission. --- ## Enforcement Points **HTTP tool calls** — before each outbound request, the engine checks `allow_http` and that the target domain is in `allowed_http_domains`. Blocked calls produce a `HttpDomainNotAllowed` violation. **Shell commands** — if `allow_shell` is false and an agent attempts a shell invocation, the call is rejected with a `ShellNotAllowed` violation before the command is spawned. **Filesystem operations** — write operations are counted against `max_file_write_bytes`. Reads beyond the allowed path prefix produce a `FilesystemNotAllowed` violation. --- ## Violation Records Every blocked operation is recorded as a violation in the execution receipt: json { "capability_violations": [ { "kind": "HttpDomainNotAllowed", "detail": "Domain 'evil.com' not in allowed_http_domains", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:00:01Z" } ] } Violation records are included in the signed receipt and cannot be removed or suppressed. Compliance auditors can verify that policy enforcement was applied to every execution. --- ## Violation Types | Kind | Trigger | |---|---| | `HttpNotAllowed` | HTTP tool called but `allow_http` is false | | `HttpDomainNotAllowed` | Domain not in `allowed_http_domains` | | `ShellNotAllowed` | Shell command attempted but `allow_shell` is false | | `FilesystemNotAllowed` | Path outside allowed prefix |

Breaking changes are marked explicitly. --- ## docs — API contract and workflow documentation — April 2026 ### Added - Explicit API support labels (`Core`, `Supported`, `Preview`) and deployment modes (`Cloud`, `Local`, `Hybrid`) across the API reference - Workflow documentation for first cloud integration, local runtime deployment, hybrid deployment, receipts and audit, and fleet rollout ### Changed - Quick Start now presents the OpenAI-compatible API as the recommended onboarding path - SDK guidance now states clearly that JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, and Rust are the current first-class native SDKs - The public API reference no longer publishes runtime-to-control-plane callback routes as customer-facing endpoints ### Migration No code migration is required. title: Circuit Breaker
description: The circuit breaker protects your inference pipeline from cascading failures when a provider degrades or becomes unavailable.
content: Circuit Breaker How It Works Closed (Healthy) Open (Unhealthy) Half-Open (Testing) State Machine Configuration What Counts as a Failure? Monitoring Console API Best Practices # Circuit Breaker The circuit breaker protects your inference pipeline from cascading failures when a provider degrades or becomes unavailable. --- ## How It Works The circuit breaker monitors provider health in real time and automatically diverts traffic away from unhealthy providers. It operates in three states: ### Closed (Healthy) The provider is operating normally. All requests flow to it according to the routing strategy. - Failures are counted but do not affect routing - When failure count reaches the threshold, the circuit opens ### Open (Unhealthy) The provider is considered unhealthy. No new requests are sent to it. - Requests are immediately routed to the next provider in the fallback chain - A timer starts — after the timeout period, the circuit transitions to half-open ### Half-Open (Testing) The circuit allows a single test request through to check if the provider has recovered. - If the test succeeds, the circuit closes (provider is healthy again) - If the test fails, the circuit reopens and the timeout resets --- ## State Machine ┌──────────┐ Success ──────►│ CLOSED │────── All requests flow │ │ └────┬─────┘ │ consecutive failures >= threshold ┌────▼─────┐ │ OPEN │────── Zero requests, timer running │ │ └────┬─────┘ │ timeout elapsed ┌────▼─────┐ Success ──────►│ HALF-OPEN│────── 1 test request Failure ──────►│ │────── Reopen on failure └──────────┘ --- ## Configuration Circuit breaker settings are configured per-tenant: json { "circuit_breaker": { "enabled": true, "failure_threshold": 5, "success_threshold": 3, "timeout_seconds": 30, "half_open_max_requests": 1, "monitoring_window_seconds": 300 } } <TypeTable type={{ enabled: { type: 'boolean', description: 'Enable circuit breaker.', default: 'true', required: true, }, failure_threshold: { type: 'number', description: 'Consecutive failures required before the circuit opens.', default: '5', required: true, }, success_threshold: { type: 'number', description: 'Consecutive successes required to close the circuit from half-open.', default: '3', required: true, }, timeout_seconds: { type: 'number', description: 'Seconds before an open circuit transitions to half-open.', default: '30', required: true, }, half_open_max_requests: { type: 'number', description: 'Maximum concurrent requests allowed during half-open probing.', default: '1', required: true, }, monitoring_window_seconds: { type: 'number'

title: Cloud Coordination
description: Overture is the cloud control plane for routing, fleet registration, receipts, and account-scoped policy.
content: Cloud Coordination Routing BYOK Vault Fleet Registration Receipts And Audit # Cloud Coordination Overture is the cloud control plane for routing, fleet registration, receipts, and account-scoped policy. --- ## Routing At request time, Overture can route inference across the configured providers and maintain provider statistics such as latency and recent request outcomes. Customer-visible routing endpoints in the current build include: - `GET /v1/routing/stats` - `GET /v1/routing/recent` - `GET /v1/routing/leaderboard` - `POST /v1/routing/strategy` Preview routing endpoints also exist for speculative routing and advisor configuration. See [API Reference](/docs/api-reference) for the exact current contract. --- ## BYOK Vault The current public vault handler accepts these provider identifiers: - `openai` - `anthropic` - `benchmark` For customer traffic, use `openai` or `anthropic`. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' --- ## Fleet Registration Runtime instances coordinate with Overture through the `/api/v1/runtime/*` contract. The stock runtime attempts registration on startup only when: - `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` is present and validates - `IGRIS_API_KEY` is present If you are implementing your own runtime launcher, the registration payload must match the current API: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/api/v1/runtime/register \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "machine_id": "edge-gateway-01", "hostname": "edge-gateway-01", "platform": "linux-amd64", "runtime_version": "1.6.0", "endpoint": "http://192.168.1.100:8080" }' Related endpoints: - `POST /api/v1/runtime/heartbeat` - `DELETE /api/v1/runtime/deregister` - `GET /api/v1/runtime/commands` - `GET /api/v1/runtime/list` --- ## Receipts And Audit The coordination layer is where customer-facing receipt queries currently live: - `GET /v1/receipts` - `GET /v1/receipts/:id` - `GET /v1/receipts/export` - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` Use these endpoints for customer audit workflows rather than assuming a separate local receipts listing API exists on the runtime. --- [Fleet Management →](/docs/fleet-management) · [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-refere

description: The Routing Advisor analyzes your routing history and proposes configuration changes — adjusting provider weights, enabling speculative execution, or switching routing strategy — b
content: Routing Advisor How It Works Proposals GET /v1/cognitive/proposals GET /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id POST /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id/apply → {"status": "applied", "applied_at": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z"} Auto-Apply Configuration GET /v1/cognitive/config PUT /v1/cognitive/config # Routing Advisor The Routing Advisor analyzes your routing history and proposes configuration changes — adjusting provider weights, enabling speculative execution, or switching routing strategy — based on observed performance. Auto-apply can be configured to apply proposals automatically when they meet your confidence and risk thresholds. --- ## How It Works 1. The advisor monitors routing telemetry continuously 2. When it detects an optimization opportunity, it generates a **proposal** with a confidence score and a risk score 3. You can review and apply proposals manually, or configure auto-apply thresholds 4. Applied changes take effect immediately; a rollback window is available --- ## Proposals ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals List pending and recent proposals. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "id": "prop-01HXYZ", "type": "routing_strategy", "description": "Switch to latency-optimized routing — Anthropic p50 has dropped 18% over 24h", "confidence": 0.91, "risk_score": 0.12, "estimated_improvement": "~18% latency reduction", "proposed_at": "2026-03-01T12:00:00Z", "status": "pending" } ] | Field | Description | |---|---| | `confidence` | 0–1 — how certain the advisor is this change helps | | `risk_score` | 0–1 — estimated risk of degradation | | `status` | `pending`, `applied`, `rejected`, `rolled_back` | --- ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id Get a single proposal with full detail. --- ### POST /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id/apply Apply a proposal immediately. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals/prop-01HXYZ/apply \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # → The change takes effect on the next request. If performance degrades within the rollback window, you can revert via the console or by applying the previous configuration manually. --- ## Auto-Apply Configuration The advisor can apply proposals automatically when they meet configured thresholds. Set `enabled: true` in the auto-apply config to activate. ### GET /v1/cognitive/config Returns the current auto-apply configuration. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/config \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "enabled": false, "confidence_threshold": 0.85, "max_risk_score": 0.25, "eval_interval_mins": 60, "rollback_window_mins": 30,

title: Console User Guide
description: The Igris console at console.igrisinertial.com is the primary web interface for monitoring your fleet, reviewing execution runs, managing agents, tuning policy, and handling billin
content: Console User Guide Dashboard Fleet → Devices Agents Execution Runs Execution Runs → Approve / Reject Proof → Violations History Behavior Tree Editor Settings → Keys Settings → Billing Related Pages # Console User Guide The Igris console at [console.igrisinertial.com](https://console.igrisinertial.com) is the primary web interface for monitoring your fleet, reviewing execution runs, managing agents, tuning policy, and handling billing. This guide walks through every section. --- ## Dashboard The dashboard is the first screen after sign-in. It shows a real-time snapshot of your tenant's activity. **Metric cards** | Card | What it means | |---|---| | Active Executions | Execution runs currently in a RUNNING or PAUSED state across all registered runtime instances | | Violations (24h) | Count of capability violations recorded in the last 24 hours | | Fleet Health | Fraction of registered instances currently reporting a healthy status | | Quota Used | Runtime instances in use vs your tier limit (e.g. 12 / 50) | **Interpreting the numbers** - A nonzero violation count is not always an emergency — single violations on test agents are routine. A spike in violations across multiple agents at the same time warrants investigation. Open **Proof → Violations** to see which capability type is being blocked and which agents are producing it. - Fleet health below 100% means at least one registered instance has stopped sending heartbeats. Open **Fleet → Devices** to identify which instance is offline and whether it is expected to be. - Quota used approaching your limit will affect whether new instances can register. If you are near the limit, consider upgrading your plan under **Settings → Billing**. **When numbers look wrong** If active executions reads zero when you expect runs in progress, verify that your runtime instances are registered and healthy in **Fleet → Devices**. Executions are counted against the instance that processed them — if an instance drops offline mid-run, the run stays in its last reported state until it reconnects. If violation count appears unexpectedly high, check whether a new agent was deployed with overly broad capability requests. Use **Agents** to inspect per-agent violation counts and identify the source. --- ## Fleet → Devices The **Devices** page lists every runtime instance registered to your account. **Device status** | Status | Meaning | |---|---| | Healthy | Instance is sending regular heartbeats. Error rate and latency are within normal bounds. | | Degraded | Instance is reachable but error rate or latency has exceeded warning thr

description: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what the model should see, what the runtime should remember, and what the product should preserve across steps, failures, and depl
content: Context Engineering Start With The Smallest Useful Context The Context Layers In Igris 1. Request-local context 2. Retrieval and memory 3. MCP and shared context 4. Durable task state 5. Receipts and audit context Choosing The Right Layer Implementation Checklist Common Patterns Hosted inference with light context Agent workflows with reusable state Hybrid deployments with shared device state Long-running workflows A Practical Product Pattern Common Mistakes What Good Context Engineering Looks Like Code And Workflow Quality Signals Related Guides # Context Engineering Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what the model should see, what the runtime should remember, and what the product should preserve across steps, failures, and deployments. In Igris, that choice matters because context can live in several different places: - the request itself - memory systems - MCP and shared context - durable-task checkpoints - receipts and audit records If you put the wrong information in the wrong layer, the system still works, but it becomes harder to reason about, more expensive to operate, and more fragile across retries, restarts, and handoffs. --- ## Start With The Smallest Useful Context The default rule is simple: give the model only the context required to succeed at the current step. That means: - put request-specific instructions and inputs in the request - put reusable knowledge in retrieval or memory - put shared operational state in an explicit shared context layer - put recovery-critical workflow state in durable tasks What you want to avoid is using the prompt as a dumping ground for everything the product knows. ## The Context Layers In Igris ### 1. Request-local context Request-local context belongs in the request payload itself: messages, task inputs, or tool-call inputs. This is the right place for information that matters only to the current call. Use this for: - the current user instruction - short-lived execution constraints - immediate tool-call inputs - one-off routing intent Do not use request-local context as a substitute for shared memory or durable state. ### 2. Retrieval and memory Use memory systems when context should survive beyond one request but does not need to become part of the durable workflow protocol. This includes: - semantic retrieval from vector memory - short-lived working state in KV-style memory - shared blackboard-style state when multiple agents need the same view Use this when the question is: "what should the next step be able to recall?" Use durable tasks instead when the question is: "what must survive an interruption and resume safely?" ### 3. MCP and shared context Use MCP when context should be shared across tools, sessions, or runtime instances in a structured way. MCP is the right layer for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented context - cross-instance context in swarm or multi-device operation Use MCP when context is part of the operating en

title: Data Privacy
description: Igris is designed with privacy as a core principle. This guide explains how your data is handled, stored, and protected across the platform.
content: Data Privacy Data We Collect Account Data Execution Data Fleet Data Provider Keys How We Handle Your Data Data Storage Data Retention Data Isolation Your Rights Data Access Data Deletion Data Portability Privacy by Deployment Mode Cloud API Mode Edge / Offline Mode Hybrid Mode Third-Party Data Sharing Cloud Providers Billing Analytics Compliance GDPR Data Processing Agreement Security Measures Contact # Data Privacy Igris is designed with privacy as a core principle. This guide explains how your data is handled, stored, and protected across the platform. --- ## Data We Collect ### Account Data - Email address and account information - Subscription tier and billing history - API key metadata (prefix only — full keys are never stored after creation) ### Execution Data - Request inputs (prompts, messages) - Model outputs and responses - Resource usage metrics (tokens, latency, cost) - Capability violations and enforcement actions - Signed execution receipts ### Fleet Data - Runtime instance identifiers and registration details - Health metrics and telemetry - Configuration state - Topic mappings (for ROS2 integrations) ### Provider Keys - Cloud provider API keys (encrypted at rest) - Key validation status and rotation history --- ## How We Handle Your Data ### Data Storage - **Cloud API users**: Execution data is stored in our managed infrastructure with encryption at rest - **Edge/Offline users**: All data stays on your device. Nothing is transmitted to Igris servers unless you explicitly export it ### Data Retention Execution records are retained according to your tier: | Tier | Retention Period | |---|---| | Seed | 7 days | | Horizon | 30 days | | Infinite | 90 days (customizable) | After the retention period expires, execution data is automatically purged. ### Data Isolation All data is strictly scoped by tenant. Your data is never accessible to other tenants, and Igris staff cannot view your execution content without explicit authorization. --- ## Your Rights ### Data Access You can access all data associated with your account at any time: - Export execution receipts via the API - Download your fleet configuration - View your complete audit log bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?range=30d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" ### Data Deletion You can request deletion of your account and all associated data: 1. Navigate to **Settings → Account** 2. Click **Delete Account** 3. Confirm the deletion Account deletion is permanent and irreversible. All execution records, fleet data, and configuration will be removed within 30 days. ### Data Portability You can export all your data in a structured format for migration to another system. Contact [support@igrisinertial.com](mailto:support@igrisinertial.com) for a full data exp

title: Deploy Local Runtime
description: Use this workflow when execution should happen on the machine itself instead of only through the hosted API.
content: Deploy Local Runtime 1. Download the runtime archive 2. Install the binary 3. Configure auth and local model behavior 4. Start and verify the runtime 5. Test a local call Common Mistakes Related Guides # Deploy Local Runtime Use this workflow when execution should happen on the machine itself instead of only through the hosted API. Choose this path when you need: - on-device inference - local policy enforcement - offline or low-connectivity operation - runtime-local behavior tree execution If those requirements are not central to the workload, start with the hosted API first. Local runtime is a deployment choice, not the default onboarding path. --- ## 1. Download the runtime archive Use the runtime distribution endpoints for your platform and treat download as a provisioning step, not as application traffic. bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-amd64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the archive checksum before installation. ## 2. Install the binary bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ## 3. Configure auth and local model behavior Create `~/.config/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0 } } ## 4. Start and verify the runtime bash igris-runtime serve curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health Use the local runtime API only against the runtime base URL, not the hosted API. That sounds obvious, but it is one of the most common integration mistakes once teams begin mixing hosted and local deployment models. ## 5. Test a local call typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'http://localhost:8080/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'phi3', messages: [ ], }); ## Common Mistakes - Pointing the client at `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` for a local-only route - Assuming local auth behaves exactly like the hosted API - Treating runtime download as a hot-path request rather than a provisioning step ## Related Guides - [Quick Start →](/docs/quickstart) - [Deployment →](/docs/deployment) - [Local LLM Fallback →](/docs/local-llm-fallback) - [API Introduc

description: Igris can be deployed as a cloud-hosted API, as a local execution engine on your own hardware, or in a hybrid configuration combining both.

Point your SDK at the API and start making requests. python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1", api_key="your-api-key" ) The cloud API handles: - High availability and failover across providers - Provider health monitoring and automatic routing - Cost tracking and budget enforcement - Upgrades and maintenance ### Self-Hosted Coordination (Infinite Tier) Deploy the coordination layer in your own infrastructure for data residency, compliance, or custom integration requirements. The coordination layer ships as a single binary with low infrastructure requirements. title: Durable Task Execution
description: Long-running agent workflows and robotics missions need to survive the infrastructure they run on. Durable task execution gives every multi-step task a tamper-evident Write-Ahead L
content: Durable Task Execution How it works Submitting a task Agent tasks Robotics missions Raw task definitions Polling task status Listing tasks Durable streaming Checkpoints and resume tokens Deadlines Robotics workflows Behavior tree execution Integrity guarantees API endpoints # Durable Task Execution Long-running agent workflows and robotics missions need to survive the infrastructure they run on. Durable task execution gives every multi-step task a tamper-evident Write-Ahead Log (WAL), periodic checkpoints, and automatic failover to a healthy runtime if the executing one goes dark. A task that was 40 steps into a 100-step workflow when its runtime crashed resumes at step 41 instead of starting over, with durable progress metadata and a signed audit trail that covers the handoff. --- ## How it works Every durable task follows the same three-layer protocol: **1. Write-Ahead Log** — Before each step executes, the runtime writes an `Intent` entry to the WAL recording the step index, type, and a SHA-256 digest of the input. After successful execution, the entry is updated to `Committed` with the output digest and an Ed25519 signature over the full entry. If the step fails, the entry is marked `Failed` with a reason. **2. Periodic checkpoints** — Every five committed steps, the runtime sends a `CheckpointPayload` back to the coordination layer. The payload contains a `ResumeToken` with the last committed step index and a rolling SHA-256 digest over all committed output digests in step order. **3. Automatic recovery** — The coordination layer scans for runtimes with stale heartbeats every 15 seconds. Any runtime silent for more than 90 seconds is marked unhealthy. Its in-flight tasks are immediately reassigned to a healthy runtime with a `ResumeToken` derived from the last persisted checkpoint. --- ## Submitting a task bash POST /v1/tasks/submit Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Content-Type: application/json Durable tasks now support two submission styles: - Typed wrappers for common agent and robotics workloads - Raw `task_definition` payloads for advanced callers who want full control The coordinator normalizes either form into the same runtime durable-task contract. ### Agent tasks Use `agent_task` when you want the coordinator to build either a `single_inference` task or an `agent_workflow` for you. json { "task_type": "agent_workflow", "agent_task": { "name": "report-q3-analysis", "steps": [ { "model": "gpt-4.1-mini", "messages": [ ], "memory": { "recall_query": "Q3 report context", "store_output": true } }, { "model": "gpt-4.1-mini", "messages": [ ], "approval": { "required": true } } ] }, "idempotency_key": "report-q3-2026-run

title: Routing Engine
description: The routing engine is Igris's provider selection system. It combines circuit-breaker logic and real-time provider health monitoring to make optimal routing decisions for every infe
content: Routing Engine What It Is How It Works Routing Strategies Adaptive (Default) Cost-Optimized Latency-Optimized Strategy Configuration Circuit Breaker Console Integration # Routing Engine The routing engine is Igris's provider selection system. It combines circuit-breaker logic and real-time provider health monitoring to make optimal routing decisions for every inference request. --- ## What It Is The routing engine is the core decision layer that powers Igris's multi-provider inference coordination. It evaluates available providers, their current health and performance characteristics, and selects the optimal provider for each request. Request → Routing Engine → Provider Selection → Inference The routing engine runs: - **In the cloud** — as part of the coordination layer, routing requests across your provider pool - **On edge devices** — embedded in the Runtime binary, making local routing decisions when multiple models or providers are available --- ## How It Works The routing engine continuously tracks performance metrics for each configured provider: | Metric | Description | |---|---| | **Latency** | p50 and p95 response times with exponential decay weighting | | **Success rate** | Fraction of requests returning valid responses | | **Cost** | Per-token cost based on provider pricing | | **Availability** | Current health status from continuous monitoring | On each request, the engine evaluates these metrics against your routing strategy to select the best provider. --- ## Routing Strategies ### Adaptive (Default) The default routing strategy automatically balances exploration (trying providers to keep statistics fresh) with exploitation (using the best-known provider). Traffic adapts in real time — a provider that degrades sees its traffic share drop automatically. When it recovers, traffic gradually returns. ### Cost-Optimized Routes requests to minimize cost per token while maintaining acceptable quality. Useful for high-volume, cost-sensitive workloads. ### Latency-Optimized Routes requests to minimize response time. Useful for interactive applications where speed is the primary concern. ### Strategy Configuration json { "routing": { "strategy": "thompson-sampling", "fallback_chain": ["anthropic", "openai", "local"] } } [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) --- ## Circuit Breaker The circuit breaker protects against cascading failures when a provider degrades: ┌──────────┐ Success ──────►│ CLOSED │────── Requests flow normally └────┬─────┘ │ consecutive failures >= threshold ┌────▼─────┐ │ OPEN │────── Reques

The Coordination Layer Routes the Request The coordination layer receives the request and applies routing logic before forwarding: **Authentication.** The API key is validated and associated with a tenant. title: Execution Model
description: Every request that passes through Igris runs inside a bounded execution envelope. This page explains how execution works from request arrival to signed receipt.
content: Execution Model Execution Envelope Capability Bounds Execution Path Cloud path Local path Hybrid path Signing Receipt Storage # Execution Model Every request that passes through Igris runs inside a bounded execution envelope. This page explains how execution works from request arrival to signed receipt. --- ## Execution Envelope When the execution engine receives a request, it opens an execution envelope before processing begins. The envelope is a structured record that captures the full execution context. An envelope contains: - **Identity**: request ID, tenant ID, timestamp - **Inputs**: the original prompt, system message, and parameters - **Capability grants**: what the execution is permitted to do - **Resource limits**: token budget, time budget, step budget - **Outputs**: model response and tool call results - **Resource usage**: tokens consumed, wall time, tool calls made - **Capability violations**: any rejected operations When execution completes, the envelope is finalized and signed cryptographically. The signature covers the canonical form of all fields. The signed envelope becomes the execution receipt. [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) --- ## Capability Bounds Before execution begins, the engine checks the request's declared capability grants against the tenant's configured policy. If the request claims more than its policy allows, the engine rejects it before the model is invoked. During execution, the engine enforces capability limits in real time: | Capability | What it restricts | |---|---| | `allow_http` | HTTP calls to external endpoints | | `allow_shell` | Shell command execution | | `allow_filesystem` | File read/write operations | | `max_tokens` | Output token limit | | `max_steps` | Maximum planning or tool-call steps | | `max_duration_ms` | Maximum wall time for the full execution | If an execution exceeds any limit, the engine terminates it and records the violation in the receipt. Violations are part of the signed record — they cannot be suppressed. [Capability Model →](/docs/capability-model) --- ## Execution Path ### Cloud path When cloud providers are configured and available: Request → Engine → Cloud provider (OpenAI / Anthropic / Google / ...) │ Response │ Engine signs receipt │ Return to caller The cloud provider runs inference. title: Execution Receipts
description: Execution receipts are the customer-facing audit record for what ran, where it ran, and whether policy violations occurred.
content: Execution Receipts Current Query Surface List Receipts Export Receipts Proof Verification # Execution Receipts Execution receipts are the customer-facing audit record for what ran, where it ran, and whether policy violations occurred. --- ## Current Query Surface The current customer query surface for receipts lives in Overture: - `GET /v1/receipts` - `GET /v1/receipts/:id` - `GET /v1/receipts/export` - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` The current runtime build does **not** expose a public local `GET /v1/receipts` listing endpoint. If you are running fully local, consume the signed `execution_receipt` data returned in responses and store it in your own workflow if you need local retention. --- ## List Receipts bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts?limit=50&violations_only=true" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Supported query parameters: | Parameter | Description | |---|---| | `limit` | Max results, default `50`, max `500` | | `from` | Inclusive lower timestamp bound | | `to` | Inclusive upper timestamp bound | | `agent_id` | Filter by agent ID | | `violations_only` | Restrict to violating executions | Current response shape: json [ { "execution_id": "exec-01HXYZ", "agent_id": "agent-abc", "runtime_id": "runtime-01", "tenant_id": "tenant-456", "timestamp_utc": "2026-03-01T12:00:00Z", "wall_time_ms": 312, "cpu_time_ms": 287, "memory_peak_mb": 48, "tool_calls": 1, "violation_occurred": false, "status": "completed", "receipt_hash": "sha256:a3f9...", "previous_hash": "sha256:b2e8...", "signature": "base64:...", "transaction_id": "txn-01HXYZ", "prompt_preview": "Evaluate whether to initiate..." } ] --- ## Export Receipts bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=jsonl&from=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -o receipts.jsonl The current export formats are: - `jsonl` (default) - `csv` Current export filtering supports: - `from` - `to` --- ## Proof Verification Use the proof endpoints when you want receipt-oriented verification views: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' --- [Audit →](/docs/audit) · [Security →](/docs/security) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

title: First Cloud Integration
description: Use this workflow when you want the shortest path from zero to a working Igris integration.
content: First Cloud Integration 1. Create a tenant API key 2. Add a provider key 3. Call the OpenAI-compatible API 4. Decide whether you need a native SDK Common Mistakes Related Guides # First Cloud Integration Use this workflow when you want the shortest path from zero to a working Igris integration. If your goal is to get a production integration live quickly, this is the path to follow. It keeps the contract simple, avoids deployment complexity, and lets you confirm the product value before you adopt deeper product surfaces. The recommended sequence is: 1. Create a tenant API key 2. Add at least one provider key 3. Call the OpenAI-compatible API 4. Move to a native SDK only when you need Igris-specific features --- ## 1. Create a tenant API key Create one tenant API key for the environment that will call the hosted API. Treat it like any other production secret and keep it in your standard secret store. - [Trial & Billing →](/docs/trial-billing) - [API Authentication →](/docs/api-reference/authentication) ## 2. Add a provider key Igris routes requests using provider credentials stored in the vault. For most customer traffic today, use `openai` or `anthropic`. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' ## 3. Call the OpenAI-compatible API This should be your default starting point unless you already know you need native SDK features or local execution. typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o-mini', messages: [ ], }); console.log(response.choices[0].message.content); ## 4. Decide whether you need a native SDK Stay on the OpenAI-compatible path if you need inference, broad language portability, and the least integration overhead. Move to a native SDK when you need: - receipt helpers - vault operations - fleet APIs - richer routing metadata The first-class native SDKs today are JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, and Rust. - [SDKs →](/docs/sdk) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) ## Common Mistakes - Starting with a preview SDK or a local runtime before proving that the hosted path already solves the use case - Forgetting to add a provider key before sending hosted inference traffic - Using a browser session flow for backend automation ## Related Guides - [Quick Start →](/docs/quickstart) - [AP

title: Fleet Rollout Workflow
description: Use this workflow when you need to manage many runtimes as one operational fleet.
content: Fleet Rollout Workflow 1. Confirm runtimes are eligible to participate 2. Inspect current fleet state 3. Push configuration deliberately 4. Roll runtime updates in stages 5. Verify post-rollout health Common Mistakes Related Guides # Fleet Rollout Workflow Use this workflow when you need to manage many runtimes as one operational fleet. This is the customer workflow for: - seeing registered runtimes - pushing configuration - coordinating updates --- ## 1. Confirm runtimes are eligible to participate Before rollout, make sure each runtime can: - start cleanly - reach the hosted product - register successfully - report health consistently If registration is not healthy, rollout is the wrong next step. Fix runtime readiness first, then come back to rollout. ## 2. Inspect current fleet state Use the fleet inventory surface before making changes. That gives you the real target set, not the target set you assume exists. ## 3. Push configuration deliberately Use config push for settings changes such as runtime behavior, local model paths, or fallback configuration. Roll configuration changes separately from binary upgrades whenever possible so failures are easier to isolate and rollback decisions are easier to make. ## 4. Roll runtime updates in stages Use OTA update controls in stages: 1. canary a small set of runtimes 2. watch health and task behavior 3. expand the rollout only after the first slice is stable Avoid all-at-once rollout unless the fleet is extremely small and the blast radius is acceptable. ## 5. Verify post-rollout health After configuration or update rollout, confirm: - runtimes remain visible - heartbeats continue - local task execution still succeeds - customer-facing traffic is unaffected ## Common Mistakes - Rolling out configuration and binary updates at the same time without a reason - Skipping canary stages - Treating runtime download and update operations like ordinary application traffic ## Related Guides - [Fleet Management →](/docs/fleet-management) - [Hybrid Deployment Workflow →](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow) - [Troubleshooting →](/docs/troubleshooting)

title: Governance
description: Igris's governance model gives you verifiable, auditable records of every AI decision. Governance applies to every execution, whether running on cloud or local hardware.
content: Governance What Governance Covers Execution Receipts Capability Model Agent Lifecycle Transaction Boundary Routing Policy Trust Chain Compliance Use Cases Setting Up Governance for Your Fleet Step 1 — Define your capability policy Step 2 — Assign policies to agents Step 3 — Monitor violations Step 4 — Review receipts for compliance Step 5 — Adjust and iterate # Governance Igris's governance model gives you verifiable, auditable records of every AI decision. Governance applies to every execution, whether running on cloud or local hardware. --- ## What Governance Covers Governance answers three questions: 1. **What happened?** Every execution produces a signed receipt with inputs, outputs, timing, and resource use. 2. **Was it within bounds?** Capability gates enforce declared limits before and during execution. 3. **Can it be verified?** Receipts are cryptographically signed and tamper-evident. --- ## Execution Receipts Every execution produces a receipt: a structured, signed record of the full execution. Receipts contain: - The original request (inputs) - The response (outputs) - Resource usage: tokens consumed, time elapsed, tool calls made - Which capability gates were active - A cryptographic signature over the canonical envelope Receipts are stored locally on the execution engine. They can be queried via API and exported for audit workflows. [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) --- ## Capability Model Igris enforces a capability model: every execution declares what it is permitted to do, and the engine rejects operations outside that scope before they complete. Capability grants control what an execution is permitted to do: | Capability | What it controls | |---|---| | `allow_http` | Whether the agent can make outbound HTTP calls | | `allowed_http_domains` | Allowlist of domains for HTTP calls | | `allow_shell` | Whether the agent can execute shell commands | | `allow_filesystem` | Whether the agent can read or write files | | `max_file_write_bytes` | Maximum bytes the execution may write | Execution resource limits (max tokens, max steps, max wall time) are set separately in your containment policy and apply regardless of capability grants. A request that exceeds its capability grant is rejected before the operation executes. The rejection is recorded in the execution receipt. [Capability Model →](/docs/capability-model) --- ## Agent Lifecycle Igris tracks the lifecycle of agent executions: creation, active execution, completion, and termination. Lifecycle events are recorded in the execution envelope and available via the observability API. For long-running agents, Igris enforces: - Heartbeat requirements - Maximum active duration - Graceful shutdown on deadline [Agent Lifecycle →](/docs/agent-l
