title: Hybrid Deployment Workflow
description: Use this workflow when you want one product experience for the customer while combining the hosted API with one or more local runtimes.
content: Hybrid Deployment Workflow 1. Keep the application pointed at the hosted API 2. Start runtimes with registration credentials 3. Verify cloud and runtime access separately 4. Use fleet APIs for coordination 5. Separate hot-path traffic from provisioning traffic Common Mistakes Related Guides # Hybrid Deployment Workflow Use this workflow when you want one product experience for the customer while combining the hosted API with one or more local runtimes. This is the right model when you want: - hosted API access for the application layer - local runtime execution close to the device or workload - fleet visibility and rollout control - a fallback path between hosted and local execution --- ## 1. Keep the application pointed at the hosted API The application-facing base URL stays the same: text https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1 That keeps the customer contract unified even when runtimes are participating underneath. The application continues to see one product API, while Igris decides where execution and coordination should happen. ## 2. Start runtimes with registration credentials Hybrid deployment only works when the runtime can register successfully. bash export IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY="YOUR_LICENSE_KEY" export IGRIS_API_KEY="YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" igris-runtime serve ## 3. Verify cloud and runtime access separately Confirm both sides independently: - hosted API calls succeed with your tenant API key - the runtime answers `http://localhost:8080/v1/health` - fleet visibility appears in the console when registration succeeds ## 4. Use fleet APIs for coordination Once runtimes are participating, use the documented fleet-management routes and workflows for: - runtime inventory - config push - OTA updates Do not rebuild a parallel coordination system when the product surface already supports it. Hybrid works best when the application path stays simple and device operations stay explicit. ## 5. Separate hot-path traffic from provisioning traffic Keep the hosted inference path and runtime management path conceptually separate: - application traffic calls the hosted API - operators and rollout systems manage runtimes and fleet operations That keeps the architecture readable, makes failure handling clearer, and avoids treating device management like ordinary inference traffic. ## Common Mistakes - Pointing application clients directly at runtime coordination routes - Expecting fleet visibility without valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` - Mixing rollout traffic and customer inference traffic into the same operational path ## Related Guides - [Quick Start →](/docs/quickstart) - [Fleet Management →](/docs/fleet-management) - [Cloud Coordination →](/do

title: Key Management
description: Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer.
content: Key Management What The Current Public API Supports Add A Provider Key Rotate, Validate, Remove Security Properties # Key Management Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer. --- ## What The Current Public API Supports The current public vault handler accepts these provider identifiers: | Provider | Intended use | |---|---| | `openai` | Customer cloud traffic | | `anthropic` | Customer cloud traffic | | `benchmark` | Synthetic or test traffic | Do not assume broader provider coverage on the public vault API unless it is explicitly documented in the current contract. --- ## Add A Provider Key bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' Current request fields: | Field | Description | |---|---| | `provider` | Provider identifier such as `openai` | | `key_name` | Human-readable name for the key | | `api_key` | Provider secret to encrypt and store | --- ## Rotate, Validate, Remove Current routes: - `GET /v1/vault/keys` - `GET /v1/vault/keys/:provider` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/rotate` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/validate` - `DELETE /v1/vault/keys/:provider` The current response contract returns masked values only. Raw provider secrets are never returned after creation. --- ## Security Properties - Provider keys are encrypted before storage - Key operations are tenant-scoped - API responses expose masked key material only - Vault operations are available through authenticated control-plane APIs --- [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) · [Security →](/docs/security) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

The shipped config supports local model loading and tuning knobs such as context size, threading, GPU layer offload, and prompt caching. json5 { local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/mistral-7b.Q4_K_M.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0, max_tokens: 512, temperature: 0.7 } } Optional fields also available in the current runtime: - `main_gpu` - `prompt_cache_dir` - `batch_size` - `lora_adapter_path` --- ## Configuration Fields | Field | Description | |---|---| | `enabled` | Enables the local fallback subsystem | | `model_path` | Path to the GGUF model on disk | | `context_size` | Runtime context window size | | `threads` | CPU threads for local inference | | `n_gpu_layers` | Number of model layers offloaded to GPU | | `max_tokens` | Default local generation cap | | `temperature` | Default local sampling temperature | There is no dedicated pure-local fallback toggle in the current runtime config. For pure local deployments, point clients directly at `http://localhost:8080/v1` and do not rely on cloud routing. --- ## Hybrid Behavior In a hybrid deployment: 1. Your application calls Overture 2. Overture routes normally across cloud providers 3. If the runtime is registered and selected by your routing configuration, local execution can participate in the request path In a fully local deployment: 1. Your application calls the runtime directly 2. The runtime answers from the local model 3. Signed execution receipts are returned with the response payload when enabled by the runtime path --- ## Supported Model Format The current runtime expects GGUF model files on disk. content: MCP Guide Pages Transport Surfaces Method Families Session and Transport Context and Resource Operations Tooling and Agent Workflows How MCP Fits In # MCP MCP is the structured context layer in Igris. Use it when context belongs to the operating environment and must move between tools, agents, sessions, or runtimes without becoming accidental prompt state. This section documents MCP as part of the product contract. Start with the overview pages below if you are orienting yourself, then move to the transport and integration guides when you are shaping production workflows. ## Guide Pages - [MCP Server](/docs/mcp-server): customer-facing transport and method model - [MCP Swarm Mode](/docs/mcp-swarm): how shared context behaves in multi-agent execution - [MCP Integration Patterns](/docs/mcp-integration-patterns): practical patterns for durable, auditable context usage ## Transport Surfaces - [`POST /v1/mcp`](/docs/mcp-server): hosted transport for customer-facing MCP requests - [`POST /v1/mcp/stream`](/docs/mcp-server): streaming transport when MCP exchange needs incremental output ## Method Families ### Session and Transport - initialize session state - advertise capabilities - establish request and response shape ### Context and Resource Operations - list available context resources - read resource content - push or refresh context into the shared working surface ### Tooling and Agent Workflows - expose tools to participating agents - share execution context across swarm members - coordinate working context without confusing it with receipts or durable checkpoints ## How MCP Fits In Use MCP for shared working context. Use durable tasks for long-running progress. Use receipts for audit evidence. Keeping those three concerns separate is what makes the system understandable and operable at scale. --- [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering) · [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

title: MCP Integration Patterns
description: This guide shows how to use MCP as part of a production integration rather than as an isolated protocol feature.
content: MCP Integration Patterns Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Related Guides # MCP Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use MCP as part of a production integration rather than as an isolated protocol feature. --- ## Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Use MCP for working state that tools, agents, or runtimes need to share. Do not use MCP as the place where audit evidence lives. Keep audit and receipt workflows separate so the system remains understandable. ## Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Avoid dumping arbitrary JSON into a few generic keys. Define stable keys and value shapes for shared context that your application team can reason about. Good: - `mission_state` - `dispatch_plan` - `device_role` Weak: - `state` - `payload` - `latest_data` ## Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately MCP and durable tasks solve different problems: - MCP shares structured state - durable tasks preserve progress and resume semantics Use both when a long-running workflow needs shared context and safe recovery. Do not force one to replace the other. ## Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Your application should still think in terms of one product: - hosted coordination when the application contract belongs in the cloud - runtime-local execution when work belongs on-device - MCP for shared operational state across those boundaries ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Durable Tasks →](/docs/durable-tasks) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

title: MCP Server
description: This page documents the MCP server surface that Igris exposes through the product.
content: MCP Server What The MCP Server Is For Customer Contract Request Shape Core Method Families Integration Guidance Related Guides # MCP Server This page documents the MCP server surface that Igris exposes through the product. The goal is to treat MCP as part of the product contract, not as an implementation detail hidden behind generic tool calls. --- ## What The MCP Server Is For Use the MCP server when context needs to move between agents, tools, sessions, or runtimes in a structured way. That makes it useful for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented working context - multi-agent coordination - runtime-local or cross-runtime context exchange If the problem is only one request deep, keep the data in the request instead. Use MCP when the context belongs to the operating environment. ## Customer Contract The customer-facing hosted entry points are: - `POST /v1/mcp` for request/response JSON-RPC calls - `POST /v1/mcp/stream` for streaming MCP interactions The product forwards those calls to the appropriate runtime MCP server where needed, so the customer can keep thinking in terms of one product surface. ## Request Shape The MCP request body follows JSON-RPC 2.0: json { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "context/write", "params": { "key": "mission_state", "value": { "step": 3, "status": "navigating" } }, "id": 1 } ## Core Method Families The main MCP method families exposed through Igris today are: - `context/*` for structured shared context - `tools/*` for tool discovery and invocation Treat the specific method contract as part of your application integration, not as an undocumented side channel. ## Integration Guidance - keep request-local prompt data out of MCP unless it truly belongs in shared state - prefer explicit keys and schemas for shared context - do not mix audit evidence with working context - use durable tasks when progress recovery matters more than context recall ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering) - [Hybrid Deployment Workflow →](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow)

title: MCP Swarm Mode
description: MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network.
content: MCP Swarm Mode What It Solves Operational Model Configuration Design Boundaries Common Mistakes Related Guides # MCP Swarm Mode MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network. Use it when context must move between devices or runtime instances without turning every exchange into an application-managed synchronization problem. --- ## What It Solves Swarm Mode is useful when: - multiple runtimes need the same operational context - one runtime should be able to continue after another runtime wrote the latest shared state - distributed planning or robotics coordination needs a shared context layer ## Operational Model In Swarm Mode: - runtimes discover peers - shared context is replicated across the swarm - reads can be served from a peer that did not originate the write That makes Swarm Mode a context-sharing mechanism, not a replacement for durable workflow recovery or audit evidence. ## Configuration toml [mcp_swarm] enabled = true discovery = "mdns" encryption_key_path = "/path/to/swarm.key" ## Design Boundaries Use Swarm Mode for shared operational state. Do not use it for: - signed audit records - long-term business data retention - progress recovery that should be modeled as a durable task ## Common Mistakes - treating swarm replication as if it were a durable checkpoint protocol - storing too much request-local prompt state in the shared swarm context - using swarm state where one runtime-local value would be simpler ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

title: Memory
description: Igris supports three memory systems: vector store for semantic retrieval, KV cache for fast key-value lookup, and cross-instance context via MCP Swarm Mode.
content: Memory Vector Store KV Cache Cross-Instance Context (MCP Swarm Mode) Agent Blackboard API GET /v1/agents/memory/ GET /v1/agents/memory/:key PUT /v1/agents/memory/:key DELETE /v1/agents/memory/:key → 204 No Content On-Device Training # Memory Igris supports three memory systems: vector store for semantic retrieval, KV cache for fast key-value lookup, and cross-instance context via MCP Swarm Mode. --- ## Vector Store The vector store indexes embeddings and retrieves semantically similar documents at query time. It gives agents access to a long-term knowledge base without including everything in the context window. **How it works:** 1. Documents are embedded and stored in the local vector index 2. At query time, the agent provides a query string 3. The vector store returns the top-K most similar documents 4. Retrieved documents are injected into the agent's context **Configuration:** json { "memory": { "vector_store": { "enabled": true, "top_k": 5, "similarity_threshold": 0.75 } } } **Supported embedding models:** - Any GGUF-format embedding model - External embedding APIs (via the HTTP tool) The vector index is stored on device. Embeddings do not leave the device unless you configure an external embedding endpoint. --- ## KV Cache The KV cache provides fast key-value storage for agent state that must persist across steps or across executions. **Use cases:** - Storing intermediate results between planning steps - Persisting agent state across tool calls - Caching frequently accessed data to reduce tool call latency **Access:** json { "kv_cache": { "set": }, "get": , "ttl_seconds": 3600 } } KV entries expire after `ttl_seconds`. The cache is local to the engine instance unless MCP Swarm Mode is enabled. --- ## Cross-Instance Context (MCP Swarm Mode) MCP Swarm Mode enables execution context to be shared across multiple engine instances. Any instance in the swarm can access context written by another instance. **How it works:** - Instances auto-discover each other via mDNS on the local network - Context is written to shared encrypted storage (AES-256-GCM) - Any instance can read context written by any other instance - Context is available within milliseconds of being written **Use cases:** - Multi-robot coordination: one robot updates mission state, others read it - High-availability: if one instance goes offline, another continues the execution - Distributed agents: agents on different nodes share a working memory **Configuration:** json { "mcp_swarm": { "enabled": true, "discovery": "mdns", "encryption_key_path": "/path/to/swarm.key" } } The encryption key is device-specific and must be dis

description: > Infinite Tier — Federated model aggregation is included with the Infinite plan.
content: Model Aggregation What It Is Architecture Aggregation Rounds Round Configuration Privacy API GET /v1/federated/status GET /v1/federated/participants GET /v1/federated/rounds POST /v1/federated/rounds/start GET /v1/federated/config PUT /v1/federated/config Console # Model Aggregation > **Infinite Tier** — Federated model aggregation is included with the Infinite plan. Igris supports federated learning across your fleet of Runtime devices, enabling collaborative model improvement without sharing raw data between devices. --- ## What It Is Model Aggregation (federated learning) allows multiple Runtime devices to train local model updates (LoRA adapters) and aggregate them into a global model improvement — all without sending training data off-device. Device A: trains local adapter ──┐ Device B: trains local adapter ──┼──► Aggregator → Global model update Device C: trains local adapter ──┘ Each device: 1. Trains a LoRA adapter on its local execution history 2. Sends only the adapter weights (encrypted) to the aggregator 3. Receives the aggregated global model update 4. Applies the update to its local model Raw execution data never leaves the device. --- ## Architecture ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer (Cloud) │ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Federated Coordinator │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ Round Manager → Aggregator → Model Distributor│ │ │ └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ │Device A │ │Device B │ │Device C │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ --- ## Aggregation Rounds Federated learning operates in rounds: 1. **Round Start** — The coordinator triggers a new aggregation round 2. **Local Training** — Each participating device trains its LoRA adapter 3. **Weight Upload** — Devices upload encrypted adapter weights 4. **Aggregation** — The coordinator computes a weighted average of all adapters 5. **Distribution** — The aggregated model is sent back to all participants 6. **Application** — Each device loads the updated model ### Round Configuration json { "federated_learning": { "enabled": true, "min_participants": 3, "round_interval_mins": 60, "max_rounds_per_day": 12, "privacy_budget": 1.0, "noise_scale": 0.1 } } | Field | Type | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `enabled` | bool | `false` | Enable federated learning | | `min_participants` | int | 3 | Minimum devices required to start a round | | `round_interval_mins` | int | 60 | Time between aggregation rounds | | `max_rounds_p

title: Multi-Tenancy
description: Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail.
content: Multi-Tenancy Architecture Isolation guarantees Tenant Identification Tenant Configuration Resource Quotas Cross-Tenant Isolation Data isolation Network isolation Key isolation Billing # Multi-Tenancy Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail. --- ## Architecture Multi-tenancy in Igris is enforced at every layer: ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer │ │ │ │ Tenant A │ Tenant B │ │ Tenant C │ Tenant D │ └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ Runtime A │ │ Runtime B │ │ Runtime C │ │ (Tenant A) │ │ (Tenant B) │ │ (Tenant C) │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ ### Isolation guarantees | Layer | Isolation method | |---|---| | **Inference** | Separate API keys, separate provider configurations | | **Execution** | Separate execution envelopes with tenant-scoped IDs | | **Data** | Tenant-scoped storage — no cross-tenant data access | | **Policies** | Per-tenant policy envelopes | | **Audit** | Per-tenant receipt chains | | **Keys** | Per-tenant vault — keys are never shared | --- ## Tenant Identification Every request is associated with a tenant via the API key used for authentication. The API key maps to exactly one tenant. There is no cross-tenant key. API Key → Tenant ID → Execution Context The tenant ID is embedded in every execution receipt, ensuring full traceability from receipt back to tenant. --- ## Tenant Configuration Each tenant has an independent configuration: json { "tenant": { "id": "tenant-abc123", "name": "Acme Corp", "tier": "horizon", "providers": ["anthropic", "openai"], "policy": { "max_tokens": 4096, "max_steps": 10, "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false }, "slo": { "latency_p99_ms": 2000, "max_cost_per_request_usd": 0.05 } } } --- ## Resource Quotas Tenants are allocated resource quotas based on their tier: | Resource | Seed | Horizon | Infinite | |---|---|---|---| | Runtime instances | 3 | 50 | 500 | | Receipt retention | 7 days | 30 days | 90 days | | Federated learning | — | — | ✓ | | SLO enforcement | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | Routing advisor | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | When a tenant exceeds its quota, requests are rejected with HTTP 429. The `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header indicates remaining capacity. --- ## Cross-Tenant Isolation ### Data isolation - Execution receipts are scoped to tenant — no tenant can query another tenant's receipts - Vector store indexes are tenant-scoped - KV cache entries are tenant-scoped -

title: Provider Health
description: Igris continuously monitors the health of your configured AI providers and uses this data to make intelligent routing decisions.
content: Provider Health Health Metrics Health Status Levels Active Degraded Unavailable Health Monitoring Pipeline Provider Health Dashboard Health API GET /v1/providers/stats GET /v1/providers/health Automatic Actions Health Checks # Provider Health Igris continuously monitors the health of your configured AI providers and uses this data to make intelligent routing decisions. --- ## Health Metrics For each provider, Igris tracks: | Metric | Description | |---|---| | **Status** | `active`, `degraded`, or `unavailable` | | **Latency (p50)** | Median response time over the last 5 minutes | | **Latency (p99)** | 99th percentile response time over the last 5 minutes | | **Success rate** | Percentage of successful requests in the last 5 minutes | | **Error rate** | Percentage of failed requests in the last 5 minutes | | **Requests/min** | Current throughput | | **Cost/request** | Average cost per request in USD | --- ## Health Status Levels ### Active The provider is operating normally: - Success rate ≥ 95% - p99 latency within SLO target - Circuit breaker is closed ### Degraded The provider is experiencing issues but still functional: - Success rate between 80% and 95% - p99 latency elevated but within 2× SLO target - Circuit breaker may be half-open ### Unavailable The provider is not usable: - Success rate < 80% - p99 latency exceeds 2× SLO target - Circuit breaker is open --- ## Health Monitoring Pipeline Provider Response → Metrics Collector → Health Evaluator → Routing Decision 1. **Metrics Collector** — records latency, success/failure, and cost for every request 2. **Health Evaluator** — computes rolling averages and determines health status 3. **Routing Decision** — The routing engine uses health data to select the best provider The health evaluation runs on a sliding window (default 5 minutes). Older data decays exponentially. --- ## Provider Health Dashboard View provider health in the Console at `/models/providers`: - **Provider cards** — status badge, latency, success rate, and last checked time - **Latency chart** — p50 and p99 latency over the last 24 hours - **Success rate chart** — rolling success rate over the last 24 hours - **Cost chart** — average cost per request over time --- ## Health API ### GET /v1/providers/stats Returns health and performance statistics for all configured providers. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/providers/stats \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "providers": [ { "name": "anthropic", "status": "active", "latency_p50_ms": 287, "latency_p99_ms": 512, "success_rate": 0.994, "error_rate": 0.006, "requests_per_m

If you are unsure where to begin, start with the hosted OpenAI-compatible API. It is the shortest path to a working production integration and the easiest path to validate product fit. Move to a native SDK when you need Igris-specific product features, and move to local runtime or hybrid deployment only when the workload truly needs on-device execution, fleet participation, or offline behavior. --- ## Prerequisites - An Igris account at [console.igrisinertial.com](https://console.igrisinertial.com) - One tenant API key (`igris_...`) from **Settings → API Keys** - For cloud routing today, provider keys for the currently supported public vault identifiers: `openai` or `anthropic` - For local runtime, a GGUF model file if you want on-device inference --- ## Option A: Cloud API This is the recommended starting path for most customers. It gives you the fastest route from account setup to a live integration, while still keeping the door open to native SDKs and hybrid deployment later. ### 1. Add a provider key The current public vault API accepts `openai`, `anthropic`, and the synthetic `benchmark` provider. For customer traffic, use `openai` or `anthropic`. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' ### 2. Stay on this path if your main goal is hosted inference with the least amount of integration overhead. Move to a native SDK when you need receipt helpers, fleet APIs, vault operations, or richer routing metadata. --- ## Option B: Local Runtime Use `igris-runtime` when the workload should execute on the machine itself: local inference, local policy enforcement, behavior-tree execution, or offline operation. If you do not need those properties, the hosted API is usually the better place to start. ### 1. Download the runtime archive Pick yo

title: Rate Limiting
description: The current shipped Overture server applies a global rate limiter of 100 requests per minute by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated 10 downloads per hour per te
content: Rate Limiting What The Current Server Enforces 429 Response Shape Runtime Download Limit Local Runtime Rate Limits Client Guidance # Rate Limiting The current shipped Overture server applies a global rate limiter of **100 requests per minute** by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated **10 downloads per hour per tenant** cap. --- ## What The Current Server Enforces In `cmd/igris-overture/main.go`, the global limiter is wired as: - one shared window: `100 req/min` by default - scoped per tenant when tenant context exists, otherwise per IP The current middleware does **not** publish rate-limit headers on every successful response. It sets rate-limit headers only on the rejection path. --- ## 429 Response Shape When the global limiter is exceeded, the current response looks like this: json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } Headers on the rejection path include: - `Retry-After` - `X-RateLimit-Limit` - `X-RateLimit-Remaining` Do not depend on `X-RateLimit-Reset` being present on successful requests in the current build. --- ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime archive downloads have a separate limit of `10/hour` per tenant on the control plane download handler. This applies to: - `GET /v1/runtime/download` - subscribed runtime download workflows behind the cloud control plane --- ## Local Runtime Rate Limits The local runtime auth config supports its own request controls: json5 { auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY", rate_limit_per_minute: 60, rate_limit_burst: 10 } } | Field | Description | |---|---| | `rate_limit_per_minute` | Maximum local requests per minute | | `rate_limit_burst` | Additional local burst budget | --- ## Client Guidance - Treat `429` plus `retry_after_seconds` as the contract - Add exponential backoff client-side - Batch receipt exports and large history queries - Do not assume tier-specific global limits unless they are explicitly published in a future release contract --- [Troubleshooting →](/docs/troubleshooting) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

title: Receipts and Audit Workflow
description: Use this workflow when you need verifiable execution history, exportable receipts, or customer-visible audit evidence.
content: Receipts and Audit Workflow 1. Run requests through the documented product surface 2. Query recent execution history 3. Retrieve receipts for audit evidence 4. Export receipts for downstream systems 5. Verify before external use Common Mistakes Related Guides # Receipts and Audit Workflow Use this workflow when you need verifiable execution history, exportable receipts, or customer-visible audit evidence. This is the right path when you need to answer questions like: - what happened - what proof exists - what should be exported - what should be verified before it leaves the product boundary --- ## 1. Run requests through the documented product surface Receipts are most useful when traffic is consistently going through the intended Igris contract. Keep integrations on documented API paths so receipts, history, and exports line up with real product behavior instead of with ad hoc internal flows. ## 2. Query recent execution history Use execution history when you want a timeline view of what happened: - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) History is useful for dashboards and investigations. It tells you what happened over time. It is not the same thing as a proof artifact. ## 3. Retrieve receipts for audit evidence Use receipt listing and detail endpoints when you need the signed or hash-linked execution record itself. This is the surface you should treat as the audit artifact, not the history stream. - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) ## 4. Export receipts for downstream systems Use `GET /v1/receipts/export` when you need to move receipt data into BI, compliance, or external archive systems. Choose NDJSON for machine pipelines and CSV for spreadsheet-oriented workflows. ## 5. Verify before external use If a workflow depends on the integrity of a receipt, verify it before using it as an external audit artifact. Verification should happen before the receipt is relied on by another system, reviewer, or compliance process. ## Common Mistakes - Treating execution history as if it were the same thing as the signed receipt - Exporting receipts without deciding on a durable downstream retention model - Skipping verification when the receipt is leaving the product boundary ## Related Guides - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Audit →](/docs/audit) - [API Errors →](/docs/api-reference/errors)

content: Robotics Deployment on Robotics Hardware ROS2 Integration Mission Execution Safety in Robotics Fleet Management # Robotics Igris runs on robotics hardware with native ROS2 integration, fleet coordination, and mission execution governance. The same execution model — bounded envelopes, signed receipts — applies to robotic agents. --- ## Deployment on Robotics Hardware The execution engine runs on embedded and robotics hardware: | Platform | Architecture | Notes | |---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4/5 | ARM64 | Edge inference | | NVIDIA Jetson | ARM64 | GPU-accelerated inference | | x86 industrial PC | x86_64 | Full-size deployment | On ARM64 hardware without a GPU, Phi-3 Mini runs comfortably at 2–4 tokens/second. For time-sensitive control loops, configure the engine to use local inference exclusively and eliminate network latency. --- ## ROS2 Integration Igris exposes a ROS2 bridge that publishes and subscribes to ROS topics. AI agents can read sensor data from ROS topics and publish decisions back to the ROS graph. **Supported ROS2 distributions:** Humble, Iron, Jazzy **Configuration:** yaml ros2: enabled: true namespace: /igris input_topics: - /camera/image_raw - /lidar/scan - /odom output_topics: - /cmd_vel - /mission_status The ROS2 bridge is governed by the same capability model as other tool use. Publish operations require `tool_ros2_publish` capability grant. Subscribe operations are read-only and require no grant. [ROS2 Integration →](/docs/ros2-integration) --- ## Mission Execution Igris uses behavior trees to structure robotic missions. A behavior tree defines the mission as a hierarchy of conditions and actions. The execution engine traverses the tree, invoking AI agents at decision nodes. **Example mission structure:** Navigate to waypoint ├── [Condition: path clear?] │ ├── [Success] → Move to waypoint │ └── [Failure] → Replan path │ └── [AI agent: generate alternate route] └── [Condition: obstacle detected?] └── [Success] → Emergency stop Behavior trees run inside the execution envelope. Each tick of the tree consumes from `max_steps`. If the tree exhausts its step budget, the mission is terminated gracefully and the receipt records the state at termination. [Behavior Trees →](/docs/behavior-trees) --- ## Safety in Robotics For physical safety in robotics deployments, Igris provides: **Execution time limits.** Missions are bounded by `max_duration_ms`. title: Safety & Containment
description: Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed.
content: Safety & Containment Containment Model Resource limits cgroup bounds (Linux) Capability Enforcement Secure Defaults Violation Handling Human-in-the-Loop # Safety & Containment Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. --- ## Containment Model Every execution runs in a containment context. The containment context applies resource limits before the model is invoked and enforces them throughout execution. ### Resource limits Limits are applied per-execution: | Limit | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `max_tokens` | 4096 | Maximum output tokens | | `max_duration_ms` | 30000 | Maximum wall time (30s) | | `max_steps` | 10 | Maximum tool/planning steps | | `max_tool_calls` | 5 | Maximum tool invocations per execution | Limits can be tightened per-tenant or per-request. They cannot be relaxed beyond the configured policy maximum. ### cgroup bounds (Linux) On Linux deployments, the engine applies cgroup constraints to the execution process: - **CPU quota**: limits CPU burst during local model inference - **Memory limit**: prevents unbounded memory growth in local inference - **I/O limits**: optional disk I/O rate limits for file-system tool use cgroup enforcement is independent of application code. An agent that attempts to consume more resources than its cgroup allows is throttled or killed by the kernel. --- ## Capability Enforcement Capabilities are enforced by the engine, not by the model. Even if the model generates output that attempts a disallowed tool call, the engine intercepts and rejects it before the call executes. The enforcement sequence: 1. Request arrives with a capability grant (or secure defaults are applied) 2. Engine validates the grant against the tenant's policy ceiling 3. Engine begins execution with the validated grant in scope 4. If the model attempts a tool call, the engine checks the grant before executing 5. If the call is outside the grant, the engine records a capability violation and rejects the call 6. Execution continues or terminates depending on the violation policy Violation events are recorded in the execution receipt. They cannot be suppressed. --- ## Secure Defaults The engine applies secure defaults when capability grants are not explicitly specified: | Setting | Default | |---|---| | `allow_http` | disabled | | `allow_shell` | disabled | | `allow_filesystem` | disabled | | `max_tokens` | 2048 | | `max_steps` | 5 | Tools must be explicitly enabled. The defaults assume no tool use is intended.

The native first-class SDKs today are JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, and Rust. Python exists in-repo but remains preview. Java, C#, and Ruby should use the OpenAI-compatible API today rather than being treated as native SDK targets. Go first-class Preferred native SDK for backend services and CLI tooling. Rust first-class Preferred native SDK for systems and embedded integrations. Python preview Available in-repo, but not yet positioned as a first-class customer SDK. Java openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native Java SDK is promoted explicitly. title: SDK Integration Patterns
description: This guide shows how to use the SDK surface in a way that is maintainable in production.
content: SDK Integration Patterns Choose The Right Client Surface First Standard Environment Variables Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Pattern: Centralize Client Construction JavaScript / TypeScript Go Rust Pattern: Separate Hosted And Local Modes Cleanly JavaScript / TypeScript mode switch Pattern: Handle Product Errors Explicitly Pattern: Keep Receipt And Audit Handling Out Of The Hot Path Pattern: Start Portable, Then Go Deeper Production Checklist Related Guides # SDK Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use the SDK surface in a way that is maintainable in production. It is not a language feature catalog. It is the set of patterns that keep integrations clean when the same product may be called in cloud, local-runtime, or hybrid deployments. --- ## Choose The Right Client Surface First Start with this decision: - Use an OpenAI-compatible client when you want the shortest path to a working integration - Use a native Igris SDK when you need product-specific features such as receipts, vault operations, fleet controls, or richer routing metadata The first-class native SDKs today are: - JavaScript / TypeScript - Go - Rust If you are in Python, Java, C#, Ruby, or another language, the safest default is still the OpenAI-compatible API unless you are deliberately evaluating a preview package. ## Standard Environment Variables Use the same environment-variable model across languages: - `IGRIS_API_KEY` for hosted API access - `IGRIS_BASE_URL` when you need to override the default base URL Recommended defaults: - hosted API: `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local runtime: `http://localhost:8080` Keeping this consistent is one of the easiest ways to make cloud, local, and hybrid deployments feel like one product to your own application teams. ## Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Do not let every handler decide whether it is in cloud, local, or hybrid mode. Create one small constructor per service and keep the auth/base-URL decision there. ### JavaScript / TypeScript typescript export function createIgrisClient() { const apiKey = process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY; if (!apiKey) { throw new Error('IGRIS_API_KEY is required'); } return new IgrisClient({ baseUrl: process.env.IGRIS_BASE_URL ?? 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com', apiKey, }); } ### Go go package igrisclient import ( "os" igris "github.com/igris-inertial/go-sdk" ) func New() *igris.Client { baseURL := os.Getenv("IGR

title: Security
description: Igris security has two distinct planes:
content: Security Authentication Tenant API Keys Console Sessions Provider Keys Policy And Capability Controls Receipts And Verification Deployment Notes Compliance # Security Igris security has two distinct planes: - **Tenant API keys** for automation and programmatic access - **Console session cookies** for browser access to the web app Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Authentication ### Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys use the `igris_` prefix and are accepted in: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Best practices: - Store tenant API keys in environment variables - Rotate them if exposed - Scope usage to the tenant that owns the key bash export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_abc123..." ### Console Sessions The web console uses Better Auth session cookies. Those cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. Do not script console session access as generic bearer authorization headers. ### Provider Keys Provider keys stored through the current public vault API are encrypted before storage and returned only as masked values. --- ## Policy And Capability Controls A restrictive starting point in the current control-plane policy model looks like this: json { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_fs_write": false, "allow_external_api": false, "domain_allowlist": [], "domain_denylist": [], "writable_paths": [], "readable_paths": [], "violation_behavior": "terminate" } Start tight, then expand based on observed violations and actual agent requirements. --- ## Receipts And Verification Customer-facing verification routes currently live on the proof API: - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` - `GET /v1/proof/violations` Example: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' --- ## Deployment Notes - The local runtime can enforce its own API key with the local `auth` config - Fleet registration is gated by a valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` plus `IGRIS_API_KEY` - For local-only deployments, point clients directly at the runtime and keep your own storage if you need offline receipt retention --- ## Compliance Igris is positioned to support compliance workflows, but the exact operational model depends on where you run the control plane and runtime. - **Data residency** depends on whether you call Overture, the local runtime, or both - **Auditability** comes from receipts, proof endpoints, and export workflows - **Least privilege** comes from capabi

title: Shadow Mode
description: Shadow Mode runs a parallel execution alongside your real execution, using a different provider or configuration, without affecting the actual output. It lets you compare providers
content: Shadow Mode How It Works Use Cases Provider Comparison Configuration Testing Quality Monitoring Configuration Shadow Comparison API GET /v1/execution/shadow Divergence Score Console Cost Considerations # Shadow Mode Shadow Mode runs a parallel execution alongside your real execution, using a different provider or configuration, without affecting the actual output. It lets you compare providers, test new configurations, and detect quality degradation — all in production with zero risk. --- ## How It Works When Shadow Mode is enabled for an agent: Request → Real Execution (enforced) ──► Response to caller ↘ Shadow Execution (observed) ──► Comparison stored 1. The real execution runs normally and returns its response to the caller 2. A shadow execution runs in parallel with a different provider or configuration 3. The shadow result is stored alongside the real result for comparison 4. The shadow execution does not affect the caller, does not consume quota, and does not trigger actions --- ## Use Cases ### Provider Comparison Run your primary provider in real mode and a candidate provider in shadow mode to compare: - Latency differences - Output quality - Cost per request - Violation rates ### Configuration Testing Test new policy limits, capability grants, or SLO configurations in shadow mode before applying them to real executions. ### Quality Monitoring Detect when a provider's output quality degrades by comparing shadow results (from a trusted provider) against real results. --- ## Configuration Enable Shadow Mode per-agent via the API or Console: bash curl -X PATCH https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/agents/agent-abc \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' Shadow configuration: json { "shadow": { "enabled": true, "provider": "openai", "model": "gpt-4o-mini", "sampling_rate": 0.1, "capture_metrics": ["latency", "cost", "quality", "violations"] } } | Field | Type | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `enabled` | bool | `false` | Enable shadow execution | | `provider` | string | — | Provider to use for shadow execution | | `model` | string | — | Model to use (defaults to provider's default) | | `sampling_rate` | float | 1.0 | Fraction of requests to shadow (0.0–1.0) | | `capture_metrics` | string[] | all | Which metrics to capture | --- ## Shadow Comparison API ### GET /v1/execution/shadow Returns paired real vs shadow execution comparisons. bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/execution/shadow?range=24h&agent_id=agent-abc" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "id"

title: SLO Enforcer
description: Igris enforces Service Level Objectives (SLOs) at the routing layer to ensure every inference request meets your latency, cost, and quality targets.
content: SLO Enforcer What It Does SLO Configuration Violation Actions `fallback` `terminate` `log_only` How Latency Enforcement Works Cost Enforcement Quality Enforcement SLO Dashboard API GET /v1/slo/config POST /v1/slo/config GET /v1/slo/compliance # SLO Enforcer Igris enforces Service Level Objectives (SLOs) at the routing layer to ensure every inference request meets your latency, cost, and quality targets. --- ## What It Does The SLO Enforcer sits between incoming requests and the provider routing engine. It evaluates each request against your configured SLOs and: - **Routes to providers** that historically meet your latency targets - **Terminates slow requests** that exceed your maximum latency budget - **Falls back** to faster (possibly cheaper) providers when the primary is degraded - **Records SLO compliance** in every execution receipt SLO enforcement is independent of the capability model — it governs *how well* the execution performs, not *what* it is allowed to do. --- ## SLO Configuration SLOs are configured per-tenant and apply to all inference requests unless overridden per-request. json { "slo": { "latency_p99_ms": 2000, "latency_p50_ms": 500, "max_cost_per_request_usd": 0.05, "min_quality_score": 0.85, "violation_action": "fallback" } } <TypeTable type={{ latency_p99_ms: { type: 'number', description: '99th percentile latency target in milliseconds.', default: '5000', required: true, }, latency_p50_ms: { type: 'number', description: 'Median latency target in milliseconds.', default: '1000', required: true, }, max_cost_per_request_usd: { type: 'number', description: 'Maximum cost per request in USD. Omit to leave uncapped.', }, min_quality_score: { type: 'number', description: 'Minimum acceptable quality score from 0 to 1.', default: '0', required: true, }, violation_action: { type: '"fallback" | "terminate" | "log_only"', description: 'Action to take when an SLO is breached.', default: '"fallback"', required: true, }, }} /> --- ## Violation Actions When an SLO is breached, the enforcer takes the configured action: ### `fallback` Immediately route to the next-best provider in the fallback chain. If no provider can meet the SLO, the request is terminated with a 503. ### `terminate` Kill the in-flight request and return an error response. The violation is recorded in the receipt. ### `log_only` Allow the request to complete but record the SLO breach. Useful during SLO tuning or when you want visibility without enforcement. --- ## How Latency Enforcement Works The enforcer tracks provider latency in real time using an exponential moving average (EMA): EMA_new = α × latency_current + (1 - α)

title: Speculative Execution
description: Speculative execution runs a lightweight draft inference in parallel with the main inference. When the draft result meets a quality threshold, it is returned immediately — before t
content: Speculative Execution How It Works When It Helps When It Does Not Help Tier Availability Enabling Speculative Execution Enable for your tenant → {"enabled": true, "updated_at": "2026-03-31T09:00:00Z"} Check current configuration Check live status Reading Analytics Simulating Before Enabling Interaction with Other Features # Speculative Execution Speculative execution runs a lightweight draft inference in parallel with the main inference. When the draft result meets a quality threshold, it is returned immediately — before the main inference completes. This reduces time-to-first-token by up to 60% for streaming requests, at no change to output quality for the workloads where it applies. --- ## How It Works When speculative execution is enabled, each incoming inference request spawns two parallel paths: 1. **Draft path** — A faster, smaller model generates a candidate response. The draft is evaluated for quality as it streams. 2. **Main path** — The configured primary model processes the request normally. If the draft meets the acceptance threshold before the main inference completes, the draft is returned immediately and the main inference is cancelled. If the draft does not meet the threshold — because the task is too complex or unpredictable for the draft model — the main inference result is returned instead. The caller always receives one response. The distinction between draft and main is not exposed in the response payload. The execution receipt records which path was used. --- ## When It Helps Speculative execution provides the most benefit in these scenarios: **Streaming responses with latency requirements.** The time-to-first-token improvement is most noticeable in streaming use cases where users are waiting for a response to begin. Draft acceptance reduces the delay before the first token arrives. **Repetitive or predictable completions.** Tasks like summarization, translation, structured data extraction, and templated generation tend to have high draft acceptance rates because the output space is constrained and the draft model handles them well. **High-throughput batch workloads where p50 latency is a key metric.** At scale, improving the median case across many requests compounds into a significant reduction in overall processing time. --- ## When It Does Not Help **Non-streaming requests.** For non-streaming calls, the latency benefit is smaller because the caller waits for the full response regardless. Speculative execution still applies, but the improvement to perceived latency is minimal. **Highly creative or open-ended tasks.** Tasks like long-form creative writing, complex multi-step reasoning, or novel problem-solving tend to have low draft acceptance rates —

description: Igris supports two multi-agent coordination patterns: Council Mode for multi-provider consensus on a single request, and Swarm Mode for orchestrating commands across your entire fl

Use it when response quality matters more than cost. ### Enabling council mode per agent bash curl -X PATCH https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/agents/agent-abc \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' ### Configuring council mode bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/routing/council \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "providers": ["anthropic", "openai", "google"], "chairman": "anthropic", "synthesis_strategy": "best_ranked" }' # → | Field | Description | |---|---| | `providers` | Providers to query in parallel | | `chairman` | Provider whose model ranks the responses | | `synthesis_strategy` | `best_ranked` returns the top-ranked response; `synthesize` asks the chairman to merge responses | ### Council analytics Query council round results: bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/routing/stats \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Council metrics in the stats response show per-round cost, latency breakdown (ranking phase + synthesis phase), and winner distribution by provider. ### Cost considerations Council mode multiplies per-request cost by the number of providers queried. description: Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can
content: Tamper-Evident Logs How It Works Chain Verification What's Recorded Export GET /v1/receipts/export Console Retention Audit Workflow # Tamper-Evident Logs Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can be altered, deleted, or inserted without detection. --- ## How It Works Each execution receipt contains: 1. **Envelope hash** — SHA-256 hash of the canonical execution envelope 2. **Previous hash** — SHA-256 hash of the previous receipt (forming a chain) 3. **Signature** — Ed25519 signature of the envelope using a device-bound key Each receipt links to the previous receipt via hash, forming a chain. Each receipt is signed with a device-bound key that exists only on the originating runtime. Tampering with any receipt invalidates its signature and breaks the chain — both of which are detected by the verification API. --- ## Chain Verification Receipts can be verified at any time to confirm chain integrity: bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/receipt-01HXYZ/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "valid": true, "signature_valid": true, "chain_intact": true, "previous_hash_matches": true } If any link in the chain is broken, verification fails and the specific broken link is identified. --- ## What's Recorded Every receipt records: | Category | Fields | |---|---| | **Identity** | Request ID, tenant ID, agent ID, device ID, timestamp | | **Inputs** | Prompt, system message, parameters | | **Outputs** | Model response, tool call results | | **Resources** | Tokens consumed, wall time, CPU/memory usage | | **Capabilities** | Grants applied, violations recorded | | **Policy** | Policy hash at time of execution | | **Routing** | Provider selected, fallback count, latency | | **Chain** | Envelope hash, previous hash, signature | --- ## Export Receipts can be exported for external audit workflows: ### GET /v1/receipts/export Export receipts in the selected format and time range. bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=json&range=7d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ --output receipts_export.json Supported formats: - `json` — raw JSON array of receipts - `csv` — flattened CSV for spreadsheet analysis - `ndjson` — newline-delimited JSON for streaming processing --- ## Console View and verify receipts at `/proof/receipts`: - Receipt listing with timestamp, execution ID, agent, device, a

content: Tools Tool Overview HTTP Tool Shell Tool Filesystem Tool Tool Audit Trail # Tools Igris agents can call external tools: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. All tool use is governed by the execution envelope's capability grants and recorded in the execution receipt. --- ## Tool Overview | Tool | Capability required | Use | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | Call external APIs, webhooks, web services | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands in a sandboxed context | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, and list files | Tools are disabled by default. Each must be explicitly granted in the request's capability grant or in the tenant's policy. --- ## HTTP Tool The HTTP tool allows agents to make GET and POST requests to external endpoints. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true }, "tool_config": { "http": { "allowed_domains": ["api.example.com", "*.example.internal"], "timeout_ms": 5000, "max_response_bytes": 65536 } } } **Security controls:** - **Domain allowlist**: agents can only reach configured domains. Wildcards are supported for subdomains. - **Timeout**: requests that exceed `timeout_ms` are aborted and the failure is recorded. - **Response size limit**: responses larger than `max_response_bytes` are truncated. If `allowed_domains` is empty, all domains are permitted. Leaving it empty is not recommended for production deployments. --- ## Shell Tool The shell tool allows agents to execute shell commands. Shell access is the most sensitive capability and should be granted only when necessary. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_shell": true }, "tool_config": { "shell": { "allowed_commands": ["ls", "cat", "grep", "python3"], "working_directory": "/workspace", "timeout_ms": 10000, "env_allowlist": ["PATH", "HOME"] } } } **Security controls:** - **Command allowlist**: only listed commands can be executed. Commands not on the list are rejected before execution. - **Working directory**: the shell is confined to the specified directory. Attempts to navigate outside it are blocked. - **Timeout**: commands that run longer than `timeout_ms` are killed. - **Environment**: only environment variables on the allowlist are passed to the child process. description: This guide covers the most common issues encountered when running Igris. For each issue you will find the symptoms, the most likely cause, and the steps to fix it.

For each issue you will find the symptoms, the most likely cause, and the steps to fix it. --- ## Runtime Not Starting ### Port already in use **Symptoms:** The runtime process exits immediately with an address binding error. Nothing appears in **Fleet → Devices**. **Cause:** Another process is already listening on the port the runtime is configured to use (default: 8080). **Fix:** Identify the conflicting process and stop it, or configure the runtime to use a different port. On Linux and macOS you can check what is using a port with: bash lsof -i :8080 After freeing the port or reconfiguring, restart the runtime. --- ### Missing API key **Symptoms:** The runtime starts but exits with an authentication error. No registration appears in the console. **Cause:** The runtime was started without a valid Igris API key in its configuration. **Fix:** Add your API key to the runtime's config file or pass it as the appropriate environment variable for your deployment method. Your API key is available in **Settings → Keys** in the console. If you do not see an API key, generate one from **Settings → Billing → Manage Account**. --- ### Config file not found **Symptoms:** The runtime exits with a message indicating it cannot find or parse the configuration file. **Cause:** The runtime is looking for its configuration file at the default path and it either does not exist or has a syntax error. **Fix:** Verify that the config file is present at the expected path. Check the file for YAML/TOML syntax errors — most runtimes print the line number of the first error. If you are using a custom path, confirm you are passing the correct path argument when starting the runtime. --- ## Runtime Not Appearing in Fleet → Devices ### Network or firewall blocking outbound registration **Symptoms:** The runtime starts and appears to be running (the local health endpoint responds) but never appears in **Fleet → Devices** in the console. **Cause:** Outbound HTTPS traffic to `overture.igrisinertial.com` is being blocked by a firewall rule, proxy, or network policy. **Fix:** Verify connectivity from the runtime host: bash curl -v https://overture.igrisinertial.com/health If this fails, work with your network administrator to allow outbound HTTPS (port 443) to `overture.igrisinertial.com`. title: Upgrade & Migration
description: This guide covers how to upgrade between Igris versions, migrate data, and handle breaking changes.
content: Upgrade & Migration Versioning Upgrading the Runtime Automatic OTA Updates (Horizon+) Manual Upgrade Compare with the checksum shown in the console Or if running directly: pkill igris-runtime && igris-runtime serve Configuration Migration Config File Format Changes Backing Up Configuration Migrating Config Fields Data Migration Execution Receipts Fleet Configuration Provider Keys Behavior Tree Definitions Breaking Changes by Version Runtime v1.8.0 (March 2026) Runtime v1.7.x (March 2026) Runtime v1.6.0 (February 2026) Runtime v0.4.0 (November 2025) Rollback Checking for Updates Via Console Via API Via CLI Support # Upgrade & Migration This guide covers how to upgrade between Igris versions, migrate data, and handle breaking changes. --- ## Versioning Igris uses semantic versioning for the runtime binary: - **Major version** (v1 → v2): Breaking changes. Requires migration steps. - **Minor version** (v1.6 → v1.7): New features, backward compatible. - **Patch version** (v1.6.0 → v1.6.1): Bug fixes, backward compatible. The cloud API is versioned independently and maintains backward compatibility within a major version. --- ## Upgrading the Runtime ### Automatic OTA Updates (Horizon+) If you are on the Horizon or Infinite tier, you can push updates to your fleet from the console: 1. Navigate to **Fleet → Devices** 2. Select the instances to update 3. Click **Push Update** 4. Choose the target version and update strategy **Update strategies:** | Strategy | Behavior | |---|---| | `rolling` | Update instances one at a time (default) | | `canary` | Update one instance first, verify health, then proceed | | `all-at-once` | Update all instances simultaneously | ### Manual Upgrade For Seed tier or manual deployments: 1. Download the new binary: bash curl -fsSL https://igrisinertial.com/install | bash Or download from **Fleet → Downloads** in the console. 2. Verify the checksum: bash sha256sum /usr/local/bin/igris-runtime # Compare with the checksum shown in the console 3. Restart the runtime: bash sudo systemctl restart igris-runtime # Or if running directly: # pkill igris-runtime && igris-runtime serve 4. Verify the upgrade: bash igris-runtime --version curl http://localhost:8080/health --- ## Configuration Migration ### Config File Format Changes When upgrading between major versions, the configuration file format may change. The runtime will log warnings for deprecated fields and use defaults for new required fields. **Before upgrading, review the changelog for configuration changes.** ### Backing Up Configuration Always back up your configuration before upgrading: bash cp ~/.config/igris/config.json5 ~/.config/igris/config.json5.bak ### Migrating Config Fields If the upgrade includes config format changes, the runtime will: 1. Log a warning for each deprecated field 2. Use the default value for new required fields 3. Continue operating with the migrated configuration After upgrading, review the config file and update any deprecated fields to their new equivalents. --- ## Da
